that Bill C-117, an act to provide borrowing authority for the fiscal year beginning on April 1,1993, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee in the Economics envelope.
He said: Madam Speaker, I very much appreciate the opportunity to speak at second reading of Bill C-117, the 1993-94 borrowing authority act.
Bill C-117 gives the government the authority to carry out its regular borrowing program for the fiscal year 1993-94. Under normal circumstances the bill requesting this authority would be tabled at the time of the tabling of the federal budget, usually in February, and the fiscal framework in the budget serves as the basis for the new borrowing authority.
However this year circumstances are not the same as in the past, as I did present an economic statement to the House in December with an update of the 1993-94 financial situation. As I indicated earlier, I will be introducing a budget shortly after we return from our Easter break.
Given that fact, it is important to have the new borrowing authority bill before Parliament before the new fiscal year begins, otherwise we run the risk of the bill not being passed before the borrowing authority runs out.
The fiscal framework set out in the economic statement in December provides the basis for both the 1993-94 borrowing authority and the 1993-94 Main Estimates.
With the December statement and the Main Estimates Parliament has all the information it needs to deal with the borrowing bill. I will discuss the main contents of the bill shortly, but first of all I would like to comment on the government's general economic and fiscal situation.
Since coming to office the government has pursued a clearly defined strategy to bring federal finances under control, improve Canada's international competitiveness and strengthen the private sector as the main engine of growth and job creation.
Our economic priority is to build confidence, enhance growth, create jobs and help Canadians adjust to the current economic changes and take advantage of new opportunities.
All our efforts have been directed at investing in growth through sound monetary and fiscal policies, opening up new markets through trade liberalization, streamlining government, reducing government intervention, the privatization of Crown corporations, the building of skills of Canadians and the encouragement of the private sector as the main basis for economic progress.
Despite the severe impact of a world-wide recession these efforts are beginning to yield positive effects. Canada's economy grew last year at a rate of about 1 per cent, however fourth quarter growth showed a strong upward trend of 3.5 per cent at an annual rate, with exports being the driving force. However, domestic demand has remained hesitant.
On the other hand there are encouraging signs, particularly with the growing competitive strength based on low inflation, the lowest in 30 years; reduced interest rates, the lowest prime rate in 20 years; and some mortgage rates at 5.75 per cent, the lowest in 35 years along with enhanced national productivity. These all augur very well.

March 26, 1993
Government Orders
This new Canadian strength is reflected in our export performance. Canadian businesses last year sold $157.5 billion in merchandise to foreign markets. That is an increase of almost 21 per cent since the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement was put in place. It also represents an increase of 11 per cent over 1991, the largest year-over-year increase since 1984.
I should indicate as well there are some rather interesting statistics I feel must be put on the record.
For example, in dealing with exports to the United States, Ontario's exports to the United States have increased by 29 per cent, from $56.4 billion in 1988 to $72.6 billion in 1992. Quebec's exports have increased by 27 per cent, from $16.5 billion in 1988 to $21 billion in 1992.
To go to my own home province of Alberta, again there has been an increase in exports to the United States since the free trade agreement came into effect. Alberta's exports to the United States have surged since the free trade agreement was put in place by rising 52 per cent, from $9.1 billion in 1988 to $13.8 billion in 1992.
In British Columbia, exports to the U.S. have increased by almost 14 per cent, from $7.4 billion in 1988 to $8.4 billion in 1992. Saskatchewan's exports have increased 44 per cent, from $2 billion in 1988 to $2.8 billion in 1992. Manitoba's exports are up 30 per cent, from $1.7 billion in 1988 to $2.3 billion in 1992. Nova Scotia's exports to the U.S. have increased by 29 per cent, from $1.4 billion in 1988 to $1.8 billion in 1992.
These are very impressive increases.
To look at some other sectors, transportation, electrical and electronic and chemical industries accounted for most of the gains of over 70 per cent recorded by Canada and the U.S. since the free trade agreement came into effect. Other sectors such as the Canadian high-tech exports to the United States grew from $6.6 billion to $10.7 billion, a gain of 63 per cent. The office, telecommunications and precision equipment component of that grew by 74 per cent. The electronics component went from $893 million in 1988 to $2.9 billion in 1991, a gain of 225 per cent.
These figures do not include the dramatic gains in exports to the U.S. which we have seen in the first 11 months of 1992. We really have chalked up an impressive increase in our exports to the United States since the free trade agreement was put in place.
We hear so often across the way that the free trade agreement has caused the so-called deindustrialization of Ontario. This is what the Canadian Manufacturers' Association has to say about that:
When the president of the CMA, Mr. Stephen Van Houten, was asked in a CBC interview how the free trade agreement had helped or hindered its members, he replied: "Oh, it has helped considerably. In fact, exports of manufactured goods from Canada to the United States have gone up 60 per cent since the free trade agreement came into force. So those who blame the free trade agreement for all of our ills and job losses frankly do not know what they are talking about. Without that business we would be in real trouble". The interviewer asked this question: "And you are looking forward to NAFTA?" Van Houten replied: "Very much so indeed. Our members are behind it; they tell us so in a 10:1 ratio".
That was right from the president of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. I happen to know as well that if he were asked what his opinion was of the GST, he would clearly say that without the GST there would not have been that kind of increase and that kind of penetration. The changing of the manufacturers' sales tax, the removal of the archaic, destructive manufacturers' sales tax has increased the competitive position of the Canadian manufacturing industry by something in the order of $3.5 billion to $4 billion.
Those are very impressive statistics. They clearly demonstrate that some of the policies we have been following are indeed working, making Canada more competitive, exporting more, generating more wealth, generating more jobs and improving the economic fortunes of all Canadians.
For the economy this year, these trends all support the view that we can meet the growth rate as forecast in the December economic statement of 2.5 per cent. As a matter of fact I am quite confident that can be exceeded.

March 26, 1993

The OECD, for example, in its forecast in mid-December predicted Canada's growth of 3.2 per cent this year and 4.2 per cent in 1994. Those are the levels that would lead the G-7 major economies.
I should say as well that Canada and the United States are clearly the leaders in terms of world growth. France is looking like its growth will be flat. The United Kingdom is still in a negative growth position, after seven or eight successive quarters of negative growth. Italy is going into a decline. Germany is expected to have negative growth. Japan is expected to have growth something in the order of 1.5 per cent to 2 per cent. Really, the promise is clearly focused on the North American situation and Canada is very much a part of it.
Still we notice that this means the over-all pace of growth will not be that encouraging, but it will be veiy competitive. It will require us to continue to improve our productivity and our competitiveness and to build upon the progress that has already been made.
Clearly an essential component of maintaining growth and economic progress, the single most critical issue that we face today in terms of determining our national potential for growth and job creation is to get a better handle on the deficit and the debt. I speak in terms of not only the federal deficit, but indeed the provincial deficits as well.
Since 1984-85 this government has taken firm action to improve Canada's fiscal framework and real progress has been made in reducing the deficit. As a matter of fact, I have said and I say so again, the deficit as a percentage of GDP has been reduced by almost 50 per cent, from about 8.7 per cent to 5.1 per cent. That is real progress and much of that progress was made notwithstanding the fact that we have been in the recession.
Much of this improvement results from the consistent spending restraint we have put in place. For example, from 1985-86 to 1992-93, the government has implemented a variety of restraint measures that have saved about $120 billion. About $120 billion have been shaved off the expenditure plans of the government. With these restraint measures in place, program spending growth averaged 4.1 per cent from 1984-85 to 1991-92 which is well under the rate of inflation.
Government Orders
By comparison, in the years 1969-70 to 1984-85 program spending grew at an annual rate of 13.8 per cent. In that period of time, the national debt increased elevenfold from about $18.5 billion to $206 billion. There was an elevenfold increase in the national debt during that period of time. That is what happens when program expenditures grow at the rate of almost 14 per cent over a period of 15 years. That is what happens when $1.33 is spent for every dollar's worth of revenue taken in. It simply cannot be sustained and we stopped that and turned it around.
As a result of this spending restraint, this year the government again will run an operating surplus in total revenues, that is, total revenues minus program spending. We have run an operational surplus every year since 1987-88 and it has accumulated. It has amounted to some $33 billion of accumulated surpluses since 1987-88.
Bear in mind when we assumed office, the operational deficit in 1984-85 was $16 billion. When that is contrasted with the previous administration, since 1987-88 we have generated a cumulative operational surplus of $33 billion. Contrast that with the period prior to 1984-85 when the administration previously chalked up a cumulative operational deficit during that period of time. The 10-year period before 1984-85 chalked up an operational deficit of $66.3 billion. If we had continued to spend along the lines of the previous administration and followed the Liberal pattern, we would have had a deficit of $82.5 billion today. We took action. To reinforce that commitment to restraint we brought in legislation, the Spending Control Act, which sets out firm ceilings on federal program spending for the period 1991-92 to 1995-96. The tough restraint measures we have put in place have held spending limits under the Spending Control Act.
Notwithstanding these efforts, the weakness of the economy in 1992 had a major effect upon government revenues and put upward pressure on the deficit. Confronted by this economic sluggishness we took strong action in December to reduce spending levels by an additional $8 billion over the balance of this fiscal year and the two years to come.

March 26, 1993
Government Orders
As hon. members know we took action to freeze the salaries of cabinet ministers, members of Parliament and those in the Public Service. I should point out that this is the sixth time since 1985 that cabinet ministers' and members' salaries have been cut or frozen.
We advanced a 5 per cent reduction in departmental operating budgets over the next two-year period. As for defence alone the combination of wage freezing and operating cuts will mean savings of $1.3 billion to the taxpayers of Canada.
We took targeted action on the unemployment insurance program. We cut 10 per cent in federal grants and contributions. We are prepared to take additional action as needed to ensure that our deficits as pledged in the December statement will hold true to form and to secure a firm, committed and credible track to get the government out of the pattern of public and international borrowing.
The December economic statement included a number of initiatives to bolster public and private investment and to encourage economic growth. As one will recall we announced support for small business, research and development and training and adjustment. I must say I am very pleased with the fact that the changes to the Small Businesses Loans Act, a very important piece of legislation, have been passed by the Senate and proclaimed into law. This will certainly help in a very tangible way our small business sector. I am very pleased to see that the banks, the Bank of Nova Scotia for example, announced they will be making loans under the provisions of the Small Businesses Loans Act at the prime rate of 6 per cent. I think this will be a real boon to the small business sector and provide additional stimulus to the small business sector for the creation of jobs.
We also undertook initiatives to improve the construction and resource sectors. We provided incentives for job creation through the UI premium holiday. We extended the successful home buyers plan that was introduced in last year's budget. We extended a number of improvements to encourage infrastructure and provide for some public expenditure to create jobs and to improve the competitiveness and productivity of our major industrial sectors. All of these measures will help the recovery and at the same time will ensure responsible action to reduce deficits.
We all know that all governments face similar fiscal pressures. I think it is important for all members and all people in Canada to recognize that deficits and growing debt are not just federal problems but are problems that are facing all administrations. For example provincial deficits have tripled over the last six years from $7.6 billion in 1987-88 to an estimated $23.4 billion this year. These deficits are being fuelled by spending increases that carry an onerous price. We only have to look at what happened when the federal government in the 1970s and early 1980s let program spending grow at a rate that eclipsed economic growth.
There is no way that the federal government could sustain program spending increases that averaged about 14 per cent a year for the 15 years prior to 1984-85. It created a debt and interest load that is punishing us today even though our government cut the average rate of program growth dramatically.
We all know that the current cost of servicing the debt is 32 cents out of every revenue dollar we take in. In other words for every revenue dollar that is taken in, 32 cents is lopped off the top to pay the interest on the cost of servicing the debt. Obviously that leaves that much less money to be spent on economic and social programs. If we do not deal with that and if we do not redress it then it will become progressively worse.
Likewise there is no way the provinces could sustain an average annual growth and program spending of 7.5 per cent. That is the level of spending their growth was increasing at. In some cases it was as high as 10 per cent. They are becoming trapped in the same vicious circle. We now see that provinces are running operational deficits as well. They obviously cannot sustain that.
However, in this regard we should all be encouraged that provinces are indeed taking action to contain spending. It is also encouraging to hear provinces indicating a renewed interest in working with each other and with the federal government to join in a national plan for restoring Canada's fiscal health.
We have been recommending this for some time. I certainly want to assure all members of the House and all the provinces that we will provide leadership action in dealing with this issue. We certainly have laid out a plan. We certainly would like to see a strategy outline with certain goals and objectives that can be achieved in a co-operative and co-ordinated fashion.
March 26, 1993

That puts this bill into context. I would now like to turn to the main elements of the bill. Bill C-117 contains three standard elements of previous borrowing bills. They are: first, the financial authority to cover financial requirements for 1993-94; second, the exchange fund account profits; and third, a contingency reserve.
The first element provides the government with the authority to cover its anticipated requirement for borrowing in order to meet the net financial requirements set out in the economic statement.
The second element of the bill provides for an amount of money to cover exchange fund account profits. These are the earnings which give rise to additional Canadian dollar borrowing requirements. Exchange fund account earnings are retained in the account and their main purpose is to provide the government with the capacity to intervene in foreign exchange markets.
The third element provides for a $3 billion non-lapsing reserve to cover contingencies. The reserve is there to cover unexpected contingencies such as foreign exchange and intervention requirements. This amount is the same as requested in borrowing authority bills over the last six years.
Bill C-117 is requesting $31.5 billion of regular borrowing authority for the 1993-94 fiscal year. This includes estimated financial requirements of $26.5 billion, projected exchange fund account earnings of $2 billion and a non-lapsing contingency reserve of $3 billion.
In line with the measure introduced in last year's legislation, Bill C-117 ensures that the 1993-94 borrowing authority may only be used after the 1993-94 fiscal year begins. This provision links the borrowing authority to the 1993-94 financial requirements even if Bill C-117 receives Royal Assent before the beginning of 1993-94.
The bill contains a standard clause stating that any unused borrowing authority granted by this bill over $3 billion will be cancelled on March 31, 1994. This clause allows the $3 billion non-lapsing contingency reserve to be carried forward into 1994-95 in case new borrowing authority is not in place by then.
There are also a couple of technical clauses that ensure the use of the borrowing authority matches the financial requirements for the year for which it was granted.
In addition, the bill provides for any unused borrowing authority for 1992-93 to be cancelled once Bill C-117
Government Orders
comes into force. Prior to this bill coming into force, the $3 billion contingency from the previous year's authority can be used between March 31 and the date the new borrowing authority takes effect.
Furthermore any portion of the $3 billion contingency reserve carried forward from 1992-93 and used during 1993-94 will be deducted from the 1993-94 borrowing authority.
I know that hon. members recognize the importance of passing this bill before borrowing authority runs out early in the 1993-94 fiscal year. We have announced the borrowing program for the first fiscal quarter to provide information to our investors and orderly marketing conditions for the large debt program.
This borrowing authority is a normal part of the operations of the government so I ask my colleagues to consider it and give it expeditious passage.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, only a month and a half ago the Minister of Finance through the parliamentary secretary asked this House to pass a bill authorizing the government to borrow a further $8.2 billion. This was supposedly to deal with the additional requirements of the government for the fiscal year beginning April 1, 1992.
Now, only a month and a half later, we see the Minister of Finance himself here again on behalf of the government asking for the authority to borrow $31.5 billion for the fiscal year beginning April 1, 1993. This is another request for substantial borrowing authority only a few weeks after a similar bill was presented to this House by the government.
I do not think the government has made a more convincing case for its financial record today any more than it did a month and a half ago when the earlier bill was presented by the parliamentary secretary.
The minister himself today has talked about the purposes of the government's financial policy. He talked about creating jobs and growth and helping Canadians to adjust. What has been the result of this government's policies? Since 1989 Canada has lost 325,000 manufacturing jobs. Unemployment has been at double-digit levels for two consecutive years and in spite of some slight improvement there are no prospects of this changing for the rest of this year and well into next year according to the government itself.

March 26, 1993
Government Orders
More than 200,000 people and firms have gone bankrupt since 1990 and 40 per cent of service sector jobs pay wages below the poverty level. Adjusted for inflation, average family incomes are no higher today than they were in 1983.
This situation did not happen by accident. I think this Conservative government has made some very basic policy errors such as fighting inflation at all costs, supporting high real interest rates and a high Canadian dollar and, in spite of what the Minister of Finance has said-I will talk more about this in a few minutes-a free trade agreement without a subsidies code or adjustment programs that contributed to the decline in manufacturing jobs and the deterioration of our industrial base in this country.
The minister has been talking about the benefits of his policies, his Conservative government's policies. But there are some other disturbing numbers in addition to those I have just put on the record which help to confirm that these policies have hurt rather than helped Canadians and their families in the last several years as well as at present and with respect to their prospects for the future.
Yesterday in The Globe and Mail Robert Sheppard wrote a very interesting but troubling column in which he said:
By now, most Canadians are probably aware that once wealthy Ontario has finally overtaken New Brunswick-in a big jump last year-to become the province with the largest share of welfare recipients among its general population.
As of last June, 17 per cent of Ontarians under 60 were receiving some form of provincial or municipal welfare. This is nearly three times the prevailing level throughout most of the 1980s, and four times what it was in the decade before.
Imagine that. In the province of Ontario 17 per cent of the population under 60 is now receiving some form of provincial or municipal welfare. What an indictment of this Conservative government's policies.
Mr. Sheppard goes on to say:
Neither Ontario nor the country can afford to let their new bases be set at the 10 per cent national range, let alone Ontario's 17 per
cent, only to be augmented by the "jobless recovery" of the next few years.
We have to note that to the extent there is recovery in this country it is tragically a "jobless recovery". No matter how much Canadian workers increase their skills there are still not enough jobs to meet the needs of those already unemployed, much less those entering the labour market.
The Minister of Finance went on at some length about his government's tax policies. He did not make clear that since this Conservative government came into office taxes for ordinary Canadians have been increased some 36 times. Today in The Globe and Mail Jeffrey Simpson wrote that:
Among the world's seven leading industrialized countries, only in Italy did tax revenues rise faster as a share of the economy in the 1980s than in Canada. In 1991, tax revenues in Canada accounted for 39.4 per cent of gross domestic product, compared with 31.6 per cent in 1980.
In 1980, Canadian taxes as a percentage of GDP were 6.5 points below Germany's and 3.5 points below Britain's. By 1991, the Canadian percentage exceeded that of both Germany and Britain by 3 points. In the same period, the gap between the Canadian and U.S. rates soared to 10 percentage points from 2, a striking difference between the world's largest trading partners.
Mr. Simpson made one of the most important points of all with respect to how this Conservative government has increased the tax burden on ordinary Canadians when he said:
What's arresting in the figures, compiled from the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, is how fast Canadian taxes have jumped in recent years. The tax to GDP ratio increased by 4 percentage points from 1989 to 1991 whereas it remained steady in France and the United States and actually dropped in Germany and Great Britain.
I do not think I have to remind Canadians that the present Conservative government has been in office for almost nine years, that is, over most of the period we have been talking about and certainly during the period between 1989 and 1991 when the tax to GDP ratio increased by 4 percentage points in only some two years. This is another indictment of this Conservative government and its record and the way it has mishandled the finances of this country, in spite of the protestations today by the Minister of Finance.
March 26, 1993

The Minister of Finance talked about the very good record of this government in handling these finances. What does the record actually say? It says that the accumulated public debt is in the area of $450 billion, more than twice as much as it was when this Conservative government took office. Is that good management of the country's affairs? No matter what the Conservatives say, the record is clear. The public debt is more than double today what it was when this Conservative government took office.
The Minister of Finance talks about the deficit. He admitted in his December economic statement that the budget deficit for the fiscal year 1992-93 would be $34.4 billion, some $6.9 billion more than had been forecast only a few months earlier in his February 1992 budget. The deficit is really not much different than when his government took office. As I said in this House in the borrowing bill debate only a month and a half ago, this government has put the Canadian economy and the Canadian people through a very high degree of pain for no real gain.
Another measure of this government's mishandling of the financial affairs of this country is the ratio of debt to our gross domestic product. When this government took office the ratio of debt to Gross Domestic Product was only 42 per cent. It is now in the area of about 65 per cent. That is a tremendous increase in the period since this Conservative government took office. It is a real deterioration from what it was when this government took office claiming that it had the answer when it came to our debt and deficit problems. Yes, it had the answer. That answer was to make things worse.
In the minister's speech today he talked about what the borrowing requirements would be used for, but he did not make clear that since this Conservative government has been in office its debt, which was once held almost entirely by Canadians, is now to an increasing and troubling extent held by borrowers outside this country. More than 20 per cent is held by borrowers outside this country, making us vulnerable to pressures that did not exist before this Conservative government took office.
These are the realities of our debt and deficit situation which the Minister of Finance conveniently ignored in his speech a few minutes ago. I can understand why he
Government Orders
ignored these figures. I can understand why he ignored these realities. It is because they paint a very different picture, a more realistic and accurate picture about this government's handling of this country's financial affairs than anything he said in his speech. We can understand why he would prefer to sweep these facts under the rug and try to pretend they do not exist. They do exist and they cannot be forgotten and they will not be forgotten by Canadians when they pass judgment on this government in the next election.
The minister went on to speak about improvements in exports which we welcome. He talked about linking this improvement with the free trade deal. What he did not mention was that 80 per cent of the exports of this country to the United States were duty-free before the free trade deal went into existence. They were already duty-free, 80 per cent of them. How can he say with a straight face that this improvement in exports was in fact linked with the existence of the free trade deal with the United States? Common sense would say that simply does not hold up if the reality is that 80 per cent of our exports to that country went there duty-free before the free trade deal was in existence.
He did not talk about how our exports improved because the dollar went down after this government for months and years supported a high dollar policy which undermined our export sector, whether we are talking about exports of resources or exports of manufactured goods. He did not talk about how our exports were helped finally by lower interest rates although they are still quite high in real terms compared to the interest rates in the United States. So there are other factors there which can account for the improvement in our exports.
Thank goodness for an improvement in our exports because according to the government's own statistical agency, Statistics Canada, if it was not for this improvement, even the weak and slow and vacillating growth we have seen would not be there because we have in this country a very weak domestic demand according to Statistics Canada in its publication the Canadian Economic Observer. That is important because domestic demand accounts for 60 per cent of the activity in our economy.

March 26, 1993
Government Orders
According to Statistics Canada if there is to be continued growth in the economy it will have to depend on a further pick-up in exports rather than an improvement in domestic demand. Statistics Canada in its current publication of the Canadian Economic Observer made clear that Canadian job growth slowed in January and February and household demands for cars and housing remained sluggish. Here I am making use of a summary of this publication in a story from Dow Jones in today's Financial Post: "Statistics Canada said that the reasons for the slump in household demand are unclear because they occurred at a time of rising unemployment and falling interest rates".
It seems pretty clear to me. I suggest that it seems pretty clear to most Canadians that household demand would not be very strong and consumers would not have much confidence about whether they should spend their money if unemployment was rising. They would not have that confidence if unemployment remains high and shows little prospect of change because of the policies of this Conservative government over the next year and the year afterward.
Yes, Statistics Canada, the government's own statistical agency, confirmed a weakness in household demand. That means the intention of individual consumers, individual families, working people, working men and women and small business people to buy. Statistics Canada confirmed weak consumer confidence and little prospect of change. The public is passing judgment through that lack of confidence and through that lack of household demand in this Conservative government's policies. That judgment is that the government has been a failure and has caused destruction and damage to the lives of hundreds of thousands of Canadians.
Just a few months ago, looking at the policies of this Conservative government, our distinguished Whip said to me: "If the medicine is so good then why is the patient still so sick?" That I thought was a statement of essential truth. If the Conservative medicine is so good then why is the patient still so sick? The fact is that the patient is still so sick because the Conservative medicine has not been good. It has made the patient sick. It has created the sickness rather than curing that sickness when it comes to the health of the Canadian economy.
This is confirmed by what Statistics Canada says about our unemployment figures. We know that fortunately they improved slightly in the past month but they are still well above double-digit levels at 10.8 per cent.
Statistics Canada said the main reason it improved was not because there have been a substantial number of new jobs but because a large number of Canadians gave up. They lost hope. They left the labour force. The total size of the labour force dropped.
If that were not the case we would not have seen any improvement in the unemployment figures at all. They are still shamefully high across this country, in my own city of Windsor and in many cities like it in every part of Canada.
The Minister of Finance has talked about how well his policies have been working as a way of justifying the continued request for borrowing by his government.
As I have said before, as with a business in the private sector, the government's revenues do not come in at the same time as its required needs for expenditures and borrowing. In using this debate on the government's borrowing bill as a way of putting on the record and justifying this government's economic policies, the Minister of Finance, while certainly a good debater and a good speaker, really has not made a convincing case at all as to why these policies deserve to be further supported by the Canadian people.
What is missing in the government's talk about its economic policies now and in the future is any commitment to economic growth. There is no real commitment as a priority to helping the economy grow, as part of the answer to its problems whether they are problems of unemployment, the yearly deficit or the accumulated public debt.
Yes, we need to have a sound basis of fiscal management. Yes, we need to have control of government expenditures. At the same time if government revenues are weak-the minister admitted that today-then they are weak because of the lack of economic growth. Without policies of government aimed at encouraging economic growth we are not going to get a handle on problems of the debt and the deficit. We are certainly not going to get a handle on the problem of high and chronic unemployment.
March 26, 1993

What we need is something that this government has not only refused to make a commitment to, in fact it has gone in the opposite direction. It is a commitment to economic growth as a priority of government policy for the purpose of dealing with the problems of the debt and the deficit. It is equally important for the need to deal with the lack of jobs for Canadians and all that means in terms of their hopes and confidence for the future.
This is an essential difference between the Conservatives and the Liberals. This is an essential difference between the government and my party because we are committed to operating in a framework of fiscal responsibility, but we want to use it for the purpose of growing the economy to provide better lives for Canadians now and in the future.
As I said earlier, Canadians, especially in the coming months, have to ask themselves: "If the Conservative medicine has been so good then why is the patient still so sick?" I know their common sense and good judgment will tell them that the Conservative medicine has been wrong for Canada because no matter what changes may come in the leadership of the Conservative Party, nothing else will have changed. The content of the package is the same bad medicine that brings sickness rather than health. It brings sickness in an economic and social sense rather than hope and confidence.
Therefore I say this minister has not made a case for the economic policies of his government and they must be rejected along with his government. I am confident that will happen in the next election. It will soon be replaced by a new, effective Liberal government working now and in the future in the interests of all Canadians.

March 26, 1993

As a result of the fact that only 50 per cent of Canadian credit card holders pay off their balances each month the accumulated outstanding debt is almost $11 billion and rising.

Madam Speaker, the total arrogance and contempt for democracy of this government is on display again.
By limiting debate on the substance of North American free trade to only two days the Conservative government is denying the people of northern Canada, and all Canadians, their fundamental right to have their concerns debated in this Parliament.
Northerners want to know how NAFTA will affect them on issues like telecommunications, water exports and local benefits from their resources.
Eighty per cent of my constituents do not have telephones, so who is going to pay to have them installed when U.S. companies cream off all the profit in the telecommunications industry? Water is the life-blood of northern Canada. Yet this agreement leaves our waters as unprotected as a baby in a snowstorm.

NAFTA is bad news for northern Canada and this government will pay a high price for muzzling this debate.

balance the books by the end of a first term. The Minister of the Environment weighed in by saying that he would cut the deficit without raising taxes or cutting social programs.

The government has a major dilemma on its hands. Today the Mexican ambassador to Canada has said that Mexico will not accept any side deal that imposes environmental or labour standards upon Mexico.
At the same time, the trade representative in the United States says on the other hand there will be no NAFTA unless there are safeguards on the environment and on labour standards. These are two totally opposite, contradictory positions.

They are being harassed at home, in the work place, at social events, at all times of the day. Why is the government refusing to step in and help these young Canadians in their time of need?
March 26, 1993

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, that is precisely what we are tiying to do and that is precisely what the Secretary of State is trying to do in working out a new arrangement with the lending institutions.
The hon. member is quite right. There have been abnormally high levels of student loans that have been in arrears. In large part it is caused by the arrangements currently in place with the financial institutions.
It is with that in mind that we are trying to change the system. There have been proposals that have been presented to the minister. She is currently examining those. I can assure the hon. member that we will take his representation into consideration.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same minister. Part of the problem is that there are no jobs. They cannot pay them back when they have no money.

One constituent in my riding, a young mother with three children, can't pay back her student loan because she couldn't get a job. She might lose her child tax credit, because she was told she could lose it as well as her income tax refund. Meanwhile, she is being harassed by a collection agency. Why does the government allow this unfair harassment of a woman and her family?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I genuinely appreciate the hon. member's emotion attached to this question. It is a serious question and I want to treat it in a serious fashion.
He should realize there is a provision under the current arrangement and there will be a provision under the future arrangement. Where there are difficulties experienced by a student there are provisions for that to be taken into account. The necessary flexibility and accommodation to help students in that regard are clearly defined there.
I would ask the hon. member to look at that to see whether those provisions would be helpful.
Oral Questions

Members of the post-secondary education community, in particular the National Advisory Group on Student Financial Assistance, were kept in the dark regarding the government proposals outlined in the request for financing the Canada Student Loans Program.
Why has the minister not consulted with them? As well, will the minister give his assurance in the House today that he will call on, consult with, listen to and implement the recommendations of the student representatives on this issue?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:

I am sure the hon. member recognizes, because of the commercial nature of these particular negotiations, one has to take that into consideration but I have been assured by the current minister that she will take representations into consideration.
What we are trying to do is improve the system. His colleague just indicated there were some deficiencies in the system. What we are trying to do is improve the system so that students will have access at reasonable cost and at reasonable cost to the taxpayer.

Madam Speaker, I would like to know what steps the minister intends to take to ensure that the banks do not reject physically handicaped people or who, because of their age, would be less likely to find a job. What does the minister intend to do to ensure that Canadian students are treated fairly?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):

March 26, 1993

She has asked for proposals. The proposals are in. They are currently being re-evaluated. Our goal is to try to ensure there is adequate access for student loans to the students at a reasonable cost, fair and equitable access at a reasonable return, a fair return to the financial leading institutions with a certain amount of necessary accountability for service in those accounts, and at reasonable cost to the taxpayer.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the minister of energy.
Recent statements have alluded to the economic viability of the oil and gas industry in western Canada. The recent signing of the Hibernia agreements with Murphy Oil and the federal government will prove vital to the Atlantic provinces' state of economic stability in the energy sector.
Can the minister advise this House of the current situation in western Canada and what the government's expectations are for the future prosperity of this industry?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member recognizes the importance of the industry in western Canada and in Canada and he is accurate in his assumptions on Hibernia.
I can inform the hon. member that activity, including bids for leases, has increased in the sedimentary basin in western Canada. I should also inform him the number of licensed wells has doubled, I believe, to 1,780 from 780 last year. I should also inform him that the increase in activity by rigs has increased 60 per cent this year over last year.
The reinvestment from cash flow will be over $5 billion this year. That is almost a 5 per cent increase in reinvestment over last year, but it is in the historic trend. Therefore, there is increased economic activity.
It is a good sign for the oil-producing part of western Canada. It is a good sign for Canada. The provincial governments and the Government of Canada should be complimented, along with the industry for the faith they have shown and the actions they have taken together to cause this increased activity.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, recently the Deputy Prime Minister made an announcement that his government was going to introduce enabling legislation to allow it to make any changes it wanted to the Crow benefit without further consultation with this House.
I would like to ask the Deputy Prime Minister when such legislation is going to be introduced. More important, why is he introducing enabling legislation? Why not a bill, a more substantive bill, that outlines exactly what his government plans to do with the Crow benefit?
March 26, 1993

It would be nice to have an opportunity to have a real discussion on an issue for a change around here.

strange, Madam Speaker, that the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott- Russell did not get up last week and complain about Mr. Jean-Claude Rivest, a Liberal who was appointed to the Senate last week. I did not hear the hon. member get up and complain.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):

Madam Speaker, a supplementary to the same minister.
The UN commission to investigate war crimes in Bosnia and Croatia cannot operate with "absolute peanuts", according to Canadian Commissioner Commander William Fenrick.
What efforts is Canada making and what is the minister doing to assure that this commission has adequate funds to do its important job?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first of all, we did offer the services of Commander Fenrick, so we are already providing some of the human resources that are required for the war crimes tribunal. We will be urging other countries to make resources available. We will also look at what will be required as this idea moves forward.
March 26, 1993

This was essentially a Canadian initiative as we raised it in London and then again in Stockholm in December. I am very pleased that the United Nations has now taken up the cause of this war crimes prosecution that I think we should follow in the future.
We will be urging the United Nations to adopt the kind of rules that are required and we will urge member nations and the UN to put the resources that are necessary into this. We are already putting our own resources into it by providing some of the people required and by helping to sponsor the conference in Vancouver.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Some time ago the minister stated publicly that there would be an opportunity for Canadians to get involved in the debate on a shift in foreign aid from humanitarian aid to Third World countries to a more economic aid package to the emerging countries in eastern Europe and Russia.
In view of the pending budget which might freeze things in stone and not give an opportunity for that debate, what forum is the minister going to provide for a lot of interested Canadians to have their views made known?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there are a couple of levels of discussion going on.
At the moment, we are looking at our over-all aid package from a number of points of view. First of all there is more aid today than there was in 1984. On balance, aid has increased. There have been some cuts as a result of earlier budgets. We are looking specifically within the framework we have today, "Sharing Our Future", on how that aid will be dispersed. We are also examining not just the changes in central and eastern Europe, but whether our aid to Third World countries should have some changes made to it.
The fundamental issue is that there are some success stories in aid. Some Latin American countries, for
Oral Questions
example, that used to be aid recipients now are more trading partners. We are looking at that kind of issue in terms of how to focus our aid program a little better in current times.
My colleague, the Minister for External Relations, and I are working closely on all aspects of our aid program. We will be appearing before committee. There will be the normal consultations with the NGO community and others once we have approved the document.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I wish to present a petition signed by a number of residents of Pembroke and Petawawa, areas that have much in common, who humbly pray and call upon Parliament to pass legislation to protect the unborn child.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, question No. 451 will be answered today.

With respect to the RCMP, (a) were any measures taken to promote altitudinal and behavioural change among male officers toward women, specifically with respect to issues of sexual harassment, gender inequities and violence against women and, if so, what are they (b) have any affirmative action programs been implemented and, if so, what are they?

March 26, 1993
Routine Proceedings

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Solicitor General of Canada):
speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
(a)
The community policing branch of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) recently published and distributed a family violence pamphlet relative to spousal assault. This pamphlet was designed to educate the general public as well as employees of the force to the issue of assaults against women in abusive relationships. It also provides a brief history of the problem and an outline of current laws designed to help and protect victims. It goes on to provide advice to victims as well as advice to anyone who might know a victim of spousal assault.
All contract divisions of the RCMP are at various stages of setting up police based victims services units usually staffed by a full time supervisor and volunteers from the community. These units provide assistance to all victims of crime, including women, and aid in the recovery from victimization related to criminal activity. These units also provide a listening ear and referrals to existing community services. After referral, a follow-up contact is made to ensure that sufficient and appropriate service has been provided. Where a community or court based victims' unit exists instead of a police based one, our detachments co-operate with these units by making referrals. Presently the force has approximately 100 police based units in existence with others coming on stream in the near future.
As part of its policing responsibilities, the RCMP has provided family violence training to its members since the early 1970s. Courses have been offered at the basic recruit level as well as at the regional in-service level.
Although no specific family violence course exists, many of the subjects related to family violence, such as sexual assaults, child abuse, and spousal assaults, have been taught as components of courses presented at both levels. In particular, the issue of sexual haraasment has been addressed in sessions of the Canadian Human Rights Act.
In addition, members of the force have participated in regional, inter-agency family violence workshops. Since 1988, 5,271 members have received training through this method.
The RCMP is participating in the federal family violence initiative, 91-95. Under this initiative our training programs have been reviewed in order to develop more comprehensive and innovative approaches to training in this area. Course development will address cultural and gender sensitivity issues.
As part of the interdepartmental response to incidents of family violence, the RCMP has promoted and conducted regional, inter-agency family violence workshops and will continue to do so throughout this initiative.
Upcoming activities include the development of scenarios for designing enhanced lecture materials, simulation training sessions and computer based, interactive training programs. These programs will reflect the force's commitment to providing policing services that are sensitive and responsive to the needs of victims and to Canada's diverse population generally.
In order to inform our membership of the RCMP's commitment toward cultural diversity and the law prohibiting discrimination on any ground, regardless of race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion and gender, the RCMP has recently distributed a brochure to all members entitled "Policing in Canada, RCMP Principles and Commitments to Diversity". The booklet is also available to the general public.
An employment equity unit was established within the staffing and personnel branch of the RCMP in 1991. Two analyst positions were created for overseeing this function.
As a result of a joint review between the RCMP and the Canadian Human Rights Commission, the development of an employment equity policy, currently being edited for publication and ultimate distribution, states:
The RCMP shall strive to change attitudes and behavioural patterns that have an adverse effect on the employment, career progression and attrition of members of designated groups.
The RCMP shall implement special measures as outlined above to prevent, eliminate or redress disadvantages that hinder the representation of designated groups.
The RCMP shall attempt to change behaviour that adversely affects participation of members of designated groups.
Under our human resource management plan for strategic issues, the following projects are in the works:
Develop a strategy which will encourage or require force personnel at all levels to ensure that committees, working groups, specialized teams/sections, consultation groups, et cetera, have representative consideration for women and other target groups.
March 26, 1993

Develop communications to force membership which is conducive to the promotion of harmony and understanding of issues relative to managing the value of diversity within the force's membership.
Develop a strategy that will encourage appropriate and uniform discipline to founded complaints against force employees where prejudice, discrimination, racism or harassment is involved.
A sensitization video entitled "Strength in Diversity" was produced to help RCMP employees deal more effectively with designated group members, including women. The video illustrates physical and attitudinal barriers that may be experienced by these employees and suggests ways in which these obstacles may be eliminated. The video was distributed to over 700 RCMP detachments.
International Women's Week, which is held annually to reflect the progress made to advance women's equality, is promoted throughout the RCMP. Information is made available and presentations are given to employees on topics such as self-defense, sexual harassment and violence against women.
All senior managers were provided with copies of "Beneath the Veneer", the report of the task force on barriers to women in the Public Service. In addition the summary of the report was made available to line managers and employees through the RCMP newsletter. All levels of management have been encourged to take positive action to implement the task force recommendations.
Departmental harassment policies for both Public Service employees and RCMP members have recently been strengthened to better inform employees and investigative bodies of the guidelines that apply, should harassment occur in the work place. Both policies will be published in the very near future.
An employment equity program has been in place for the Public Service component of the RCMP since 1983. The recruitment, promotion and retention of women are monitored regularly. To ensure that women have opportunities to enhance their careers and broaden their experience, a number of initiatives and policies have been implemented, for example a career advancement course for women, an assignments for career enhancement program and a part-time employment policy.
(b) Over and above the aforementioned response to question (a) the RCMP is in the process of forming focus
Government Orders
groups in the divisions to set up a networking system for female members.
In a continuing attempt to reduce imbalances and the under-representation of women within the RCMP, two special programs were sanctioned in 1988 and 1992. Under these initiatives 17 females members will have been promoted to the rank of corporal for instructor positions at the RCMP training academy by the end of 1993: 8 were processed from 1988 to 1991 and an additional 9 will be processed in 1993.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Mazankowski that Bill C-117, an act to provide borrowing authority for the fiscal year beginning on April 1, 1993, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee in the Economics envelope.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1993-94 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we have a situation in front of the House of Commons today which is shameful and unacceptable. We have a government asking this House for permission to borrow over $31 billion on behalf of the people of Canada despite the fact that this government has not presented to the House of Commons a budget for this fiscal year that is coming up.
The minister has suggested in his comments this morning that what he is asking for is permission to borrow based on his economic statement of December 1992. In fact he has already put through a borrowing authority bill based on that particular economic statement which passed in this House just a month and a half ago.

March 26, 1993
Government Orders
There is absolutely no justification that we can see for a government to come before the House of Commons and present a demand to the House of Commons that it be given carte blanche to go out and borrow over $31 billion without telling the people of Canada why that money is necessary, or without giving them any sense of the fiscal parameters within which that borrowing will take place. It has done so without giving to the people of Canada any sense of what kinds of policy directions the government will take to try to deal with the massive unemployment problems we have in this country, to try to deal with what some people have called a debt crisis in this country, or to try to deal with problems of poverty in this country that are getting seriously worse. We have no suggestion from the government as to how it will proceed to put in order the finances of this country.
Let me go back to the budget of February 1992. This is a budget that was presented by this same minister to the House of Commons, the same House of Commons, less than 14 months ago. It was presented on February 25, 1992, 13 months ago almost to the day.
Let me remind the House what was suggested within that budget from 1992. It suggested first that the deficit for 1993-94, that is this coming fiscal year for which this borrowing authority is put before us, would be a deficit, and I quote from page 71 of the budget from last year, of $22.5 billion. That would be the deficit. The financial requirements that this government would need according to this budget presented just 13 months ago were $13.3 billion. Yet today the minister is bringing before us a borrowing authority for over $31 billion.
How can any member of this House of Commons react with any sense of responsibility to an outlandish demand for authority to borrow $31 billion when just 13 months ago this same minister was telling us he was only going to need to borrow $13.3 billion? How is it possible for anybody in the country to believe what this minister is telling us today?
Clearly there have been things that have changed but we do not know what those things are. We do not know what the government's projections are for 1993-94 because we have not received a budget yet for 1993-94 despite the fact this government promised it faithfully.
Michael Wilson was the finance minister of this country. He was somebody who-whatever criticisms I have made of him-at least knew something about economics and the market in this country. At that point the government promised there would be a budget presented each February so that provincial governments, private businesses, households and all of us as members of Parliament would have some sense of where we were heading and what the government saw in the future.
However, now we have a Minister of Finance who does not understand economics, does not understand the needs of the marketplace, does not understand the concerns of Canadians across the country with respect to the debt problems we face and does not understand the concerns of provinces and we do not have a budget.
It is almost the end of March. April 1 is next week and there is no budget. We are told there will not be a budget until April 21. Yet the government asks us: "Despite the fact we have not given you a budget, write us a blank cheque for more than $31 billion and a month from now we will let you know what it is for. A month from now we will let you know what the situation will be financially in Canada during the year for which we will already have received the authority to borrow this more than $31 billion". It is absolutely and totally irresponsible.
This government talks about fiscal responsibility. It talks a good fight. Right from the day it was elected in 1984 it said it was going to deal with the deficit and the financial problems facing this country.
Well, those problems are worse in 1993 than they were in 1984 because we now face a situation where we have a government presenting demands for borrowing authorities without even presenting a budget to us.
I do not see how anybody in this House of Commons who believes in financial responsibility could vote for a borrowing authority under these circumstances. I say this to the backbenchers of the Conservative Party: If hon. members in the Conservative Party expect to go out into an election later this year and to run in their various constituencies on the fact that they have tried to get the finances of Canada in order, how can they possibly do it when they passed a borrowing authority for over $31 billion without even having a budget to go with that borrowing authority?
March 26, 1993

I warn those members that the people of Canada will not buy that kind of irresponsibility. The people of Canada are not prepared to give away blank cheques any more. They want to know what is happening. They want to know why it is happening and this government is not giving any answers at this stage whatsoever.
The minister talked in his comments about a number of other points. I want to deal with some of those points. As I say, I think the major problem with the minister's presentation was his failure to offer any satisfactory justification for getting the right to borrow more than $31 billion without a budget.
He also talked about the federal government being prepared to offer leadership in dealing with the debt problems of this country. The fact is that there have been requests from provincial governments across this country for a First Ministers' meeting on debt in Canada and this government has refused those requests. This government has refused requests coming from provinces that are hard pressed and hard hit financially and need to have a first ministers' meeting on debt. This government has said no.
Again, the people of Canada must not accept that this government really seriously cares about debt. It is willing to play politics with debt but it will not come out and try to deal with the problem seriously in a first ministers' meeting.
This government suggested that its record was superb on dealing with debt and the deficit. In that case how can it explain one of the conclusions from the C. D. Howe Institute this past February when it held its now famous workshop on avoiding a crisis? These were the proceedings of a workshop on Canada's fiscal outlook. The workshop brought together some of the foremost authorities on debt and fiscal management in this country. How can it explain that one of the strongest criticisms made in the report of the proceedings of that workshop indicated that the workshop was: "critical of the government's fiscal performance, in particular its loose stance during the late 1980s". I am quoting from page 3 of the workshop's conclusions.
The government likes to get up and blame everything on the Liberals. I admit that sometimes that is easy to do
Government Orders
or often easy to do because the Liberals left a sorry mess when they left office finally in 1984. However, the fact is that this government, the Conservative government, is being criticized by this C.D. Howe analysis. It is not the Liberal government of the time before 1984 because, let us face it, these guys may have done a bad job way back then but that is not the issue now. The issue now is what the Conservatives who have been in power for almost nine years have done.
The Conservatives have, according to this C.D. Howe analysis, clearly made a mess of things. They have created a fiscal situation by their irresponsibility in the late 1980s that has made the debt crisis in this country very much worse than it otherwise would have been.
There is no way the Minister of Finance, though he squirms and tries to cast the blame off onto somebody else, and this government can get out from under that criticism. There is no way it can escape from carrying the can for the fiscal problems we now face as a country.
The Conservatives try to blame the provinces. Listen to this government. In fact we heard it repeated today during Statements by Members. Somebody from the Conservative Party got up and said: "We have increased our transfers to the provinces". So when the provinces blame the federal government for transfers being cut back, somehow they are not being fair.
I want to quote from as neutral and disinterested a source as I could possibly find: the Dominion Bond Rating Service. This service has downgraded and put on alert the financial and debt situations of all our provinces in Canada. It outlines here the reasons why it has done that. It says one of the reasons is the effect of the recession. I am not surprised.
However, look at the second reason it cites. I quote it specifically again: B. "Federal caps or limits on the growth of all federal transfer payments". That is not the premier of Ontario. That is not the premier of New Brunswick. That is not the premier of British Columbia talking. That is the Dominion Bond Rating Service saying to the people of Canada that this federal government has created a big part of the problem that the provinces are now facing.

March 26, 1993
Government Orders
There is no way, although he might squirm and wriggle, this Minister of Finance can get out from carrying that can. There have been serious mistakes made by this government. It has made mistakes by cutting taxes to those at the top and thereby worsening our deficit. It has made mistakes by fiscal irresponsibility in the late 1980s that have been identified by the C. D. Howe Institute. It has made mistakes by cutting back the amount of money going to the provinces as the Dominion Bond Rating Service has indicated. That has thrown our provinces right across Canada into crisis.
Yet this government comes before us today and says: "We are managing the economy magnificently. Give us a blank cheque for more than $31 billion to go out and borrow".
Undoubtedly the trained seals on the Conservative side will get up and support this. Undoubtedly it will not prove to be possible for voices of reason to stop this craziness on the part of the government benches.
We have a government that has been wrong on its budget projections it made just 13 months ago. It was so wrong when it said 13 months ago that it would need just $13.3 billion. It now says it needs over $31 billion.
This government has been so irresponsible that it has not brought a budget forward to justify this borrowing authority. This government has been so vicious to the provinces that even the Dominion Bond Rating Services has underlined that as a major problem for the provinces.
This is finally a government that has been recognized even by the C. D. Howe institute as being a major part of the problem in creating the debt crisis we face in this country.
There is no way our party could ever support giving this government with this record a blank cheque for more than $31 billion in borrowing authority. This government has been so irresponsible that it deserves to be thrown out and not thrown money.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be splitting my time with the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace. I will go ten minutes and five and he will follow with ten minutes and five.
As much as I respect my hon. colleague and am delighted to share my time with him, I would like to have had more time to press home some of my points, but I am sure my hon. colleague will do equally well in pressing home the difficulties we have with this bill.
I am going to say at the outset that I have great difficulties with not only the details of this bill but with the principle involved.
Looking at it in its simplest, mundane, ordinary day-to-day terms, this is like me asking you, Mr. Speaker, to sign a blank cheque in any funds available to finance my record of financial mismanagement over the last eight and a half years. I want a blank cheque from you to continue financing the ways in which I have practised over a period of time, which have been unconscionable, and I am still not financially solvent.
If I went to a bank with the record of this government and asked for a loan, even with a guaranteed support and a demand loan where I had assets or promissory notes to cover what I was asking to borrow, I do not think it would let me get beyond the second question. It would look at my record and would boot me out on my behind.
This is a litany and it is becoming tiresome for people who watch this on channel 18, 19, 20 or whatever it is. The role of the opposition is to press home just how atrociously the government has managed the finances of the country, and I am not one who presses home with such direct and consistent criticism on a particular point.
When we have a government that over the past eight and a half years has been pressing home a pledge and a promise to put Canada's fiscal house in order, reduce the annual deficit, and retire the public debt, on a regular basis, in 1984, 1985, 1986, et cetera, the government management of the economy has been atrocious, maladroit and inept. Why? It is because over that period of time it has increased taxes 38 times including the hated
Government Orders
and badly timed goods and services tax. It has nickel and dimed students. It has reduced unemployment insurance safety nets for those people who need them the most at this particular time. It has introduced temporary surcharges that are still in existence and it is at its wits' end.
It cannot tax any more because it is well beyond the break even point of taxing individuals, and it cannot find money anywhere else. Now it has to go and borrow money. There are a number of things that bother me about this.
Borrowing money is not unusual. I think we all from time to time have to borrow money. When people borrow money surely one of the things their bank manager, assistant bank manager or whoever is going to lend them the money will look at is their credit rating and how much money they make; in other words, what they are looking at is their ability to repay the loan. That is the concern.
In 1984 when this government first looked at borrowing money the relationship of how much the country owed to how much the country made, in other words the ratio of the debt to the gross domestic product, was 42 per cent. Those are the best figures I can get and they have been verified by other people. It might be 40 per cent or 45 per cent, but it was in the vicinity of 40 per cent. We owed 40 per cent of what we made.
Eight and a half years later a concerted effort was promised by this government in its annual statements in the budget. Normally it is in February, March or April, the spring of each year, as is common for any government. It certainly has been a precedent with the Canadian government and in Parliament for as long as I can go back in my history books. There were promises by the government that it would retire this debt. It now says that the annual deficit is the same as it was when we started the exercise back in 1984 and that has caused the national debt to be doubled.
What is more important in terms of the relationship of one to the other, how much we owe versus how much we make, is that we have now gone from 42 per cent to 64 per cent. In other words, looking at our ability to pay and our financial solvency, we now owe 64 per cent of what we make.

Government Orders
Mr. Speaker, if you were running a business or were in a private situation in which you were borrowing on a regular basis 40, 45, 50, 55, 60, or 65 per cent of the money you made and you had a personal or financial debt for your business which in eight and a half years more than doubled then I do not think you would be a very good financial risk.
More important, and more scary to me and of more concern to the Canadian public, is the very question of where this is going to lead: Will the government have us in a position by the election, which has to happen by the end of this year, in which any party that assumes the custodianship of the country will never be able to take us out of the depth of financial despair we are now in?
We all know there was an attempt in 1990 to help retire the debt by changing the tax structure from essentially a manufacturers' sales tax on around 20,000 businesses in the manufacturing sector to a consumption tax on all individuals.
We all know a tax of that nature has a greater impact on those with less income because the amount they spend on necessities is much higher proportionately than for those in the higher income bracket. By having a consumption tax we attack those people who can least afford it.
The other aspect of this issue is, quite apart from the pros and cons and the advantages and disadvantages of a consumption tax not being harmonized with the 10 provinces, that the timing could not have been worse. I am sure the government's financial advisors in the country and our financial friends outside the country would have advised, and indeed had advised, against implementing a consumption tax when the government by its own admission and at its own hand was responsible for an impending made in Canada recession.
Mr. Speaker, would you expect me, with this background, knowledge and understanding, or anybody else with these concerns to be supportive of this bill? I think not.
In summary, we have a situation in which the government is asking to borrow $31.5 billion, and I wonder how
much of that is offshore contributing to our 30 per cent of foreign debt. The government is asking to borrow $31.5 billion before a budget has been put in place and further play into the promise and pledge that it is going to reduce the deficit and the federal debt.
I do not believe it for one moment. I certainly am not going to support it because I think it is wrong, and I think it is atrocious. I do not think the Canadian people will support it either.
