speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill to give the government the authority to borrow certain moneys gives us the opportunity to discuss the economic situation in this country and the government's economic policy.
Whenever we in the opposition and groups outside this House, economic experts, business experts, and think-tanks, attempt to bring to the government's attention that the economic situation in this country is bad and that its economic policy is not working, the government gives us two standard replies:
First, it trots before us a whole set of statistics attempting to show us that everything is absolutely fine, that the situation is really great, it is really moving in the right direction and so on. The second answer we usually get from government members, particularly the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, is that things were worse in the recession of 1981-82.
Let me deal with that response first because it is continually thrown back at us. Whether or not the recession we have had for the last three years is better or not as bad as the one of 1981-82 is irrelevant to the many thousands of Canadians who are unemployed now. Those kinds of answers from the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance give no comfort to those many people who are unemployed, to the many businesses that are going bankrupt, and to the many people who are living in poverty. It does not become a government of this country to use that kind of response when we seriously raise the plight of unemployed Canadians and the dire straits of our Canadian business situation.
March 26, 1993

Let me just for a minute compare the recession of 1981-82 with the present recession. Many experts, not members of this House, have pointed out that if the participation rate in our labour force stayed at what it was in 1981-82 the unemployment rates would be much higher. For example, I refer to the Ottawa based company Informetrica which in its monthly economic review in January said the following: "The disappearance of hundreds of thousands of workers is all that has kept the unemployment rate from exceeding the level reached a decade ago in what was the deepest downturn since the dirty thirties. Unemployment would have reached 13.7 per cent last year, slightly higher than during the 1981-82 slump, had 345,000 discouraged workers not given up looking for jobs".
You are only counted as being unemployed in the official unemployment statistics if you are actively looking for work. If you are not actively looking for work and have become disillusioned, frustrated, and continually turned away, and have not looked for work in the last few weeks, then you are not counted as unemployed. Because of the situation today the participation rate in our labour force is much lower than it was in 1981-82 and consequently the unemployment rates appear to be lower.
In addition those who are unemployed in this recession have been unemployed longer. In 1981-82 there were high rates of unemployment but those people found new work quicker than they are today.
The unemployment today, to a much greater extent, is based on structural changes in our economy and not cyclical types of unemployment. Consequently a structural problem in our economy, which means the closing down of factories that have existed for years and years, and replacement by automation or new trade patterns and so on, requires a different kind of solution from the cyclical type of unemployment we had for the greater part of 1981-82.
There was another major difference as well. In 1981-82, faced with high unemployment, the Liberal government of the day believed the government could and should do something. We did try to do things. We tried to kick-start the economy. We had public works programs. We had programs to build houses, infrastructure and so on, all to kick-start the economy.
Government Orders
This government was influenced by the economic policies that were promoted in the United States under President Reagan and in Britain under Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher. Their belief was that the market economy would solve all our problems and the less government did the better.
We do not believe the entire solution or the basic solution can be found by government but we believe there is a role for government. We submit that the greatest areas of prosperity in this country have been where government, in a wise partnership with the public sector, has produced a lot of jobs and a lot of growth.
The new Government of the United States recognizes that as well. It campaigned on a rejection of Reagan-Bush type economic policies and won. Now it is trying to return to what can be more properly called a mixed economy approach.
Another response we get from the government is that everything is fine, that there is a glowing picture out there. It cites certain inflation figures and points out how low inflation is, how certain trade figures are up and so on.
Whenever statistics that deal with improvements or with things getting worse are cited, the distance of improvement depends on the starting point. I could take issue with the government on many occasions for picking starting points that were misleading and false in order to show that things had greatly improved. That aside, the fact of the matter is that things are not fine economically speaking. They are not. The government can try to paint as rosy a picture as it can, but that is simply not being bought by Canadian people throughout this country.
The unemployment rate is well over 10 per cent. There are still 1.5 million Canadians unemployed. Bankruptcies during the last year have been at record levels. There are record levels of Canadians going to food banks and soup kitchens. There is a greater number of people living under the poverty line. Things have been worse in the last 10 years than they have ever been in a continuous trend since the end of the Second World War.
When the government brought in some of these policies we warned it that those policies would result in exactly what has happened. They would exasperate what might otherwise be a shallow recession or downturn in the economy. But it went ahead with them anyway.

March 26, 1993
Government Orders
We in the Liberal Party are in favour of freer trade. Our history shows that as a party we have always taken steps through GATT and otherwise to expand trading opportunities. Before the free trade agreement there was a movement between Canada and the United States to lower tariff barriers.
We opposed vigorously the so-called free trade agreement which was much more than a free trade agreement. It allowed us to be left open to all sorts of attacks on our economy from the United States. We said it would lead to high unemployment, and it did. We said it would lead to the closing of Canadian companies, and it did. It was the same with the GST. We opposed the GST. Even those economists who supported the GST said it was the wrong time, that we should not bring in a big tax increase when the country was moving into a recession.
I do not have enough time, but I could quote from article after article which back up what I have just been saying. Let me say what we have put forward time and again. The Federation of Canadian Municipalities was here this week asking the government once again to participate in a tripartite program to rebuild Canadian municipal infrastructure: roads, sewage systems, bridges, tunnels, ports and transportation systems, which would improve the economic climate of cities attract business and commerce to cities, and at the same time put thousands of people to work. Why will it not do that?

speechtext:

For a government that says it wants to stay the course on reducing the debt and the deficit this must seem to ordinary people out there watching us, and to those of us who like to think we have some common sense in here, just a little bit contradictory not to say hypocritical. However, sometimes we all borrow money because we have important purchases to make and important things to do. We want to invest in our children's education. The time has come to buy a new home and we know we are going to be building up our capacity to enjoy the future and to enjoy more security in the future. Let us have a look and see if that in fact is what the government is going to do with this $31.5 billion it is borrowing today.
First, where is it going to borrow the money? Is that borrowing going to help Canadians and Canada?
We know it has increased our foreign borrowing to the point where $22 billion in interest is going out of this country every year, outside Canada, out of the Canadian economy, away from where it can stimulate economic growth, job creation, research and development for Canada and for our economic future.
This government has us to the point where we are now sending $22 billion of that annual deficit outside Canada. That is bad enough, but another interesting point is that on the $22 billion nobody in Canada is paying tax. Not only are we sending $22 billion outside the country, but assuming a 50 per cent income tax rate we are also giving up $11 billion in income tax we could be earning on that $22 billion of interest. We have a further drain on the Canadian economy.
March 26, 1993

As I said sometimes it makes sense to borrow money. It depends on what is to be done with it. What is the government going to do with it? What is the biggest problem confronting Canada now? What is the biggest problem confronting Canadians? What is the biggest worry of our young people or of people in middle age who suddenly find themselves without jobs and not knowing how they are going to pay for their mortgages or rent or put food on the table?
A job, I think, is the biggest worry of most Canadians. Turning to unemployment in this country, 11.6 million Canadians are without jobs. There five million Canadians in total either on unemployment insurance, welfare, or living in a household where the income earner is on unemployment insurance or welfare. Where is the government's job creation program? Surely that is what it wants this $31.5 billion for.
It does not have a job creation program. It thinks this level of unemployment is just fine and that somehow Canadians will have to struggle through it and survive as best they can. It has just finished telling those same Canadians who are without jobs that the unemployment insurance they have paid into all their lives is not going to help them out much and is going to help out fewer people.
Is it going to help our young people who have never yet had jobs because they happened to come out of school at a time of high unemployment? Is this government going to be using this $31.5 billion to invest in more student loans and student grants to help young people get better education and better training so they have a future? No. In fact it is planning to give up all responsibility for the student loan program.
We all know that this past year the government started charging young people who are poor enough to qualify for student loans a fee for the loans. They do not have enough money to go to university so they qualify for the loans but now they have to pay a fee to get the loans.
Older people in our country are worried about the future of medicare and about the future of their pensions. Is this government planning to use this $31.5 billion to ensure the security of the old age security scheme or to ensure the future of medicare? No, that is not in its plans either.
Is the government planning to reduce taxes? Is it planning to do anything about those 37 different tax
Government Orders
increases it has imposed on Canadians in the last nine years that have created a large part of the economic difficulty we have by taking purchasing power out of the hands of consumers? No, that is not what it is planning to use this $31.5 billion for either.
Is it planning to improve government services so that people are not waiting two, three or four years to have a family member join them from the country they emigrated from?
Is it planning to improve services to Canadians so seniors are not waiting six months? After spending weeks on the telephone unable to get through busy signals, they are forced to go down to visit an office because there are not enough staff and there is not enough equipment to give Canadian seniors the pensions they are entitled to. No, that is not how it is planning to spend it either. It is not planning to add more public servants to deliver the service seniors really want. It becomes pretty difficult to go downtown three or four times, since they cannot get through on the phone, just to try to qualify for pensions they are entitled to because they have contributed to them all their lives.
Is the government planning to put this money into solving the problems of the environment? No, it is not. It has just gone through cutting the green plan. In fact the green plan has been a better example of cutting than of curing. From the time it was introduced in 1991 it has been steadily drained and bled of funds to solve our environmental problems. The estimates tabled just a few weeks ago show further cuts to the green plan.
Is the government planning to invest in research and development? No. It has been a steady slice away at research and development, slice away at the opportunities for the future for this country and slice away at our ability to compete internationally because we are in the forefront of key sectors of new knowledge.
As I said at the beginning sometimes it makes sense to borrow. It makes sense when we have good, positive, important things we want to accomplish. In the four years I have been in this House I have yet to hear one good positive thing that the government wants to accomplish for Canada. I have seen the cut of this, the destruction of that, the ruination of the other, and I wait yet to see one positive thing.

March 26, 1993

That is why I will say no to borrowing $31.5 billion. I do not think the government needs it because it does not have a plan to use it for the benefit of Canada.

Madam Speaker, I am always entertained by the hon. member's comments. I am delighted that I was able to get into the House to hear what he had to say.
I was disturbed by the content of what he said and I want to say that as an economics lecture this presentation we just had was totally misleading, although it was a lot of fun.
As a matter of fact, in the American basketball championships we are apparently down to the final 16 and it reminded me a little bit of these basketball coaches we see on the sidelines waving their arms around and so on. It is a lot of fun watching them but I do not know whether there is any content to it. It is really the players out there who are scoring the baskets.
What disturbed me about his comments was that he was completely misleading when it came to the debt. I think he believes profoundly in what he just said so I want to turn him around and see if he will confess to not understanding, and after listening to me perhaps he will understand exactly what happened.
He said when the Liberals were the government they had a $220 billion debt and they were able to fund it internally through Canada Savings Bonds and Treasury Bills. Through Canadians more or less buying the debt
Government Orders
we kept the money funnelling within Canada. That was his basic argument and he is quite right. About 90 per cent of our debt was funded internally, and about 10 per cent of it was denominated in foreign currencies: Tokyo, New York, Europe, wherever.
Then he argued that what has happened now with the debt, which has occurred since we have been the government, is that we have had to go outside home, outside the household and get other people to finance our debt. That was his argument.
I want to tell my hon. friend that the reality is that when we borrowed $220 billion at home until 1984 to finance the excesses of the Trudeau government during very good times we had reached the limit of our capacity to borrow at home from Aunt Nellie, Uncle Oscar, mom and dad, and brother and sister. We had reached the limit. That is what happened. The trouble was the previous government had put all sorts of people on the payroll, had all sorts of projects under way and left us with a $38 billion deficit in 1984 alone.
If we had come in and the next day decreased that to zero then hundreds, thousands of people would have been left without jobs, projects, and contracts. Therefore we could not turn that around all in one year, so we have tried to decrease the deficit steadily. In fact in 1993 it is now half the size of what it was in 1984 in relation to the size of the economy. It is very important to remember that $38 billion in 1984 was in a pie, called the Canadian economy, half the size of the pie we now have. Therefore a $30 billion deficit is half the size of what it was nine years ago.
Here is the point. We have had to borrow offshore in order just to pay the interest on this home debt that accumulated until 1984. As a matter of fact, that is all the deficit is. We have really been paying for interest on the debt we inherited, and that adds up to today's deficit. With our own operations we have run a surplus. By running a surplus on our own operations we are able to pay down the deficit even more than we would if we just broke even. The hon. member has to realize the reason we have had to go offshore to finance our debt is because we have reached the limits of financing it only internally.

March 26, 1993
Government Orders
Then he mentioned interest rates and said when we are financing internally we can set our own interest rates. No economist believes that. We have always had to maintain interest rates internally, the same as they are internationally. My hon. friend knows that and I think he should go back to economics 100 and have the reality clarified for him. I am making this intervention so he can respond to it. I always look forward to his responses, but I hope he stands up and admits he made a fundamental error in understanding economics.

One further thing, to clear up this business of credit. Standard and Poor's announced its most recent credit rating for Canada. That is on paper money. Granted, we do not borrow much in that form but we dropped. The province of Ontario with an NDP government now has a negative rating. The province of Newfoundland, supposed to be the poorest in Canada but now with a good Liberal government that knows where it is going, is now positive.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am delighted to have the opportunity to say a few words on this borrowing bill.
I wish we could get our statistics right. I have a written, signed statement from the former Minister of Finance, the Minister for International Trade, indicating that at the end of fiscal 1984 the total accumulated debt was less than $168 billion. I like that signed statement so much I have circulated it throughout my riding. Why did I circulate it throughout my riding? I did so because
government members have a tendency to inflate that figure in order to make themselves look better.
Either the minister did not tell the truth or he told the truth, and I believe he signed a true statement. It was less than $168 billion, the hon. minister said so. He signed it.
Let us look at the situation as it is today. We say the deficit is much better than what it was. It was predicted to be less than $30 billion. It is in excess of $30 billion. The debt now is over $450 billion.
Our colleagues from the government would like to make us believe that if we took that less than $168 billion debt in 1984 and factored in the interest, it would now account for the debt today. It is not true.
I have had three independent sources do that and it is absolutely totally false. It is only recently that the government has been spending in such a way that their program spending is less than what they take in so I think it is very important.
A point that is often forgotten is that there have been almost 40 tax increases and the revenues of government used to be approximately $70 billion. It is roughly $130 billion and that would have doubled if it had not made a major fiasco of its economic policy, if the recession had not set in and if the GST had yielded what it thought it would. However there has been almost a $60 billion increase. We have to look at that.
We have to look at how much more money is being made today and not just the increase in the debt. If we look at how much more it is making today and how much more that debt has in fact increased over time then how can it possibly stand up there and pretend and say without blinking an eye that it has managed well?

Let us ask Canadians whether they think this is good management. The Conservatives came to power with a debt of less than $168 billion and revenues of $70 billion and today they have a debt of $450 billion and have nearly doubled government revenues. Is that good management? Certainly not.
March 26, 1993



Their financial predictions have been off time and time again.

If they are fair, and some of them are, my hon. colleagues will admit.

The government boasts of the control of its expenditure levels, particularly of late. It tosses out these figures of 2.4 per cent and up. These figures are probably correct. I have no reason to doubt they are but one must ask how this came about. It was by cutting back transfer payments to provinces. That has been one major way. It was with the clawback and with the eradication of certain universal programs.
Let us look at the reductions and cuts to health and education. Between 1986 and 1995 there will be roughly $30 billion fewer dollars for health and education: $20 billion less for health and about $10 billion less for education. That was put on the backs of the provinces and the provinces put it on the backs of the universities, the colleges and the hospitals and the taxpayers.
It is the same as if I were to say: I have debts. [Translation]
I could go home this evening, and tell my wife and children: "We are going to divide these debts in two. You take half." Then I could start telling everyone: "I liquidated half my debts." Of course I did. I shifted the tax burden to my wife and children.
The government shifted the tax burden to the provinces, colleges, universities and hospitals. That is what happened. That is why it can say, with some measure of truth, it controlled costs.

I have a final point. I know that some other colleagues want to join in the debate and I am looking forward to the questions. In fact I would be delighted to receive the questions.
The government has undertaken cuts in a number of areas that I think are very serious: seniors' programs, official languages programs-les langues officielles, women's programs, programs for the handicapped and programs for aboriginal peoples. These are some of the
Government Orders
groups that are the most powerless in society and I am offended by that kind of approach.

I will conclude my speech, because I think some of my colleagues would like to ask some questions and I would like to answer them.
I think there is an hon. member on my left who would appreciate the time to make some comments. Provided he does not pick on the Liberals, I would be glad to share my time with him.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do not understand why the hon. member says we cut transfer payments to the provinces. If we look at the government's record from 1984 to the present day, transfer payments have increased annually. They may not have increased as fast as the provinces would have liked, but they did increase.
We must not forget one thing. I have been listening to the debate since we started this morning, and they say we need a job creation program based on public works, because it will generate jobs.
Where is the money supposed to come from? We must not forget, while we sit here as members of the House of Commons in our well appointed chamber, that the taxpayers are sitting in the gallery. If we do not tax them at the provincial level or the municipal level, is the federal government going to tax them? Come on. In the end it is still the same taxpayer who watches us on television. When we have financial problems, the federal government has to tighten its belt and the provinces have to do the same.
A few years ago the government of Ontario thought it could deal with its financial problems by running up a horrendous debt. In the process it created a demand for dollars on the international market because it had to borrow. The money came from countries like Switzerland and Japan. This put pressure on money markets and had a negative impact on the economy. And the same taxpayer is still paying the shot. If public works or students do not pay back their loans and we have to do it for them, the federal government gets the money from the taxpayers, who do not want to spend that money on their education or pay their municipal, school or provincial taxes. We will have to give them a break sometime.

Government Orders

Madam Speaker, I definitely want students who have a job and have the money to pay back their loans. I want to make that absolutely clear. I asked a question in the House today about what could be done for students who don't have a job and who are being harassed by collection agencies that are trying to recover this money.
An infrastructure program has been proposed by the leader of my party. If these people were working, if I am not mistaken, it would pay them about $17,000 or $20,000 per year. If these people on unemployment insurance or welfare were put to work, they would pay taxes, contribute to the economy and not be a drain on the federal Treasury and other resources.
I would like to refresh the memory of the hon. member who is very fair and explained more or less that what I call a cut is actually a reduction. I can live with his definition, but on this Friday afternoon when the sun is shining I would like to say, with all due respect for the spirit of friendship within these precincts, that the Prime Minister of the party in power today said several times that he would never tamper with the transfer formula. But he did. Yes, it is right there in his public speeches. Not only did he tamper with it, he reduced it by 2 per cent and again by another percentage point. He froze transfers, and this has been a real nightmare.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to be able to join in this debate for the last seven or eight minutes of the time that is allotted to this debate. I have been listening to the debate for most of the day. I am always amazed to see the Liberals and Tories ram heads with one another over who is going to provide the best economy and who will be the best economic managers of the state.
The fact is that neither of them has done what anyone would call an admirable job. Certainly to be more realistic they have done a disastrous job of handling the economy.
It has not been the New Democratic Party in power that has run up a debt of some $420 billion, which is soon to be $451.5 billion as we pass this borrowing bill in the next few days. As I stated earlier in the day I am always surprised when I hear Tories and Liberals saying how the
New Democrats cannot manage or handle an economy. In fact we have not created the problem in this country at all.
I am from a province that has been one of the hardest hit during these economic times and certainly over the history of this country. Saskatchewan has suffered dearly. When the CCF government of Tommy Douglas came to power in 1944 it was a time when the province could not even borrow a dime. It was the CCF, the reigning socialists, that brought the economic situation in Saskatchewan under control and provided opportunities for farm families, small businesses and education. It was Tommy Douglas who modernized the province of Saskatchewan. It was not the Liberals. It certainly was not the Tories. The record is very strong.
We lost power in 1964 and the Thatcher government took over. Ross Thatcher's Liberal government was in for seven years. Although it did not do as much destruction as the Devine government did later, it still left a mess.
The Allan Blakeney government came into power in 1971 and was in power for some 11 years. During that period Saskatchewan saw some unprecedented growth in that province. In fact it was in 1981 when Diane Francis-I am not sure which columnist it was but it was certainly one of the columnists on the right wing of the political spectrum-made a comment that the New Democratic government in Saskatchewan was not only the best managed government in Canada but was the best managed government in North America. It was a well run government and it was done on social democratic principles. He did it with a surplus budget besides that.
What happened in 1982? The Tory government came in under Grant Devine. People made ridiculous comments: "There is nothing wrong with this economy. One can afford to totally mismanage the Saskatchewan economy and still break even". That is what Devine said. He ran a deficit budget every single year he was in power. In the meantime he sold off Crown corporations, sold off provincial assets and cut funding to all types of organizations that were trying to help the disadvantaged and the poor and so on in that province. That was the Devine record.
March 26, 1993

When the Roy Romanow government took over in 1991 it had a situation that was a disaster. The province was $15 billion in debt. There were 980,000 people to pay off a $15 billion debt that was created almost exclusively by the Devine government that was supposed to have managers and Tories who could manage the economy. He has a masters degree in economics. My God. What a disaster.
Now the Roy Romanow government in power is faced with some very difficult situations. It is this government that has faced up to the fact that if the deficit is not cut in the province of Saskatchewan then we simply will not be able to borrow money. In fact we are so close to the precipice that in fact the federal government has put in a contingency plan in case we cannot borrow money.
The Roy Romanow government has cut the deficit from $980 million from the last year of the Devine government to $590 million last year. It is going to cut it to $390 million this year. In three years it is going to have a balanced budget. This is being done by the socialist hordes and the people who cannot manage an economy.
One simply has to look at the Saskatchewan government for an example of how to manage an economy. Even the Deputy Prime Minister has given some credit to Roy Romanow.
We have not been doing it the same way that rightwing Liberals and Tories have managed it. We have still managed to put money aside for the socially disadvantaged. We have actually increased payments to social assistance in Saskatchewan. We increased funding for a child hunger program. It is not enough. I must say that I have been critical myself of some of the things the provincial government has done but it is certainly miles ahead of anything any Liberal or Tory government has done in this country. It provided increased funding for low income seniors and it increased home care funding by 20 per cent. It has increased foster care rates by $2 million.
It set out a situation where it had some modest tax increases this year. It was not income tax. It has said that
Private Members' Business
there will be no more tax increases unless of course the government decides to do some more off-loading on to the provincial government.
I sit here in the House and hear Liberals and Tories banter back and forth about who can manage the economy better.
I would say that both of them have set really poor examples. Neither of them has a very good record on handling the economy. I think both these members on the government side and members on the opposition side would do well to take a look at Saskatchewan and its economy and take some lessons from the Saskatchewan government, which is not perfect but is certainly way ahead of anything I have seen on either side of this House or in any other province in Canada.

speechtext:
That Bill C-217, an act to provide for the review of postal rates and services and to amend certain acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee in the Departmental envelope.
He said: Madam Speaker, I am pleased to move Bill C-217 in the House of Commons this afternoon. I am happy to see the member for Manicouagan here in the House. He also represents a rural riding. I also see the member for Beauhamois-Salaberry. They will understand the need for such a bill.
Why do we need Bill C-217? Let me indicate what others said in the past.

Private Members' Business

I want to quote from a press release dated June 27, 1988 which says: "Setting up a system that gives Canadians a voice in the planning of postal rates and services is an idea whose time has come". I quote further from the same person: "Now that Canada Post is breaking even", as it was at the time, "and revenues are coming out of the pockets of postal users, customers have a right to a say in both national and local issues".
Do you want to know who said that, Madam Speaker? It was the government House leader of today. If the government House leader, for whom I have such respect, said this was right I know it has to be right because the member for Calgary Centre would certainly not lead us astray on an important matter such as providing this kind of a service to Canadians.
When the minister made this announcement on June 27, 1988 he did so with great fanfare, telling us how important it was for Canadians to have a postal services review committee.
On August 15, 1988 the then Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, today the government House leader, introduced the Postal Services Review Board Act. I must confess something here. Bill C-217 that I have introduced today is plagiarized. Yes, I know that it is a sinful thing but it is, word for word, the bill that was introduced by the now government House leader, the then consumer and corporate affairs minister.
Therefore the government across the way cannot say this bill is unreasonable. The government cannot say this bill is undesirable or unworthy of support, not after the quotes from the government House leader that I read in the House earlier today.
Why do we need a structure like that, apart from the reasons just invoked, that the minister said was a good idea? We need the bill because Canadians need to have an agency to review the activities of Canada Post. The government across the way tells us Canada Post is a Crown corporation and it cannot interfere with its operation. On the other hand, Canada Post has by law of this Parliament a monopoly on many of its services. The government does not control it by its own admission. Canada Post has a monopoly on first class mail and has a monopoly on many of the services it offers.
We have in effect an unregulated monopoly in Canada right now. That is wrong. That is not the fault of the employees and many of the officials at Canada Post. That is an error in judgment on the part of the government. That is why we need an agency of the Government of Canada, an agency of the taxpayers of Canada to oversee the operations of the post office and to provide the post office with some direction.
Let me give an example of one of the things that I find wrong. I received a letter just today. I finished answering the correspondence at the back only moments ago. A female constituent from Maxville, a senior citizen, wrote to me saying roughly the following: "Mr. Boudria, I live in a rural area just outside the village of Maxville. I used to get the postal box for $6.10 a year. Now they charge me close to $60 for the rental of that postal box. It is wrong".
I had a conversation with her and explained to her that Canada Post looks at it this way: "You are given an opportunity to have mail free at your gate if you want to install a box there". The lady quite appropriately answered: "What good does that do me, as a person living alone, a woman and a senior citizen? Am I going to go out there and shovel snow or put the mailbox back on the post when the snow plough knocks it off in the middle of winter?" That is not a reasonable thing for that person. Yet those rates for the mailboxes are approved with the input of no one.
The price of stamps goes up every year. It is approved by Order in Council of the cabinet. Four ministers sign a stack of these every morning and then it is gazetted with no input from Canadians at all. That is not right.
Then there is the whole issue of cross-subsidization. I brought proof to a parliamentary committee some years ago that Canada Post was using some of its monopoly revenue to cross-subsidize other services that it offers in which it is in competition with the private sector. That surely is not right.
It is wrong for two reasons. First of all, why should someone who is paying for a postage stamp be subsidizing some bigwig at Canada Post who has it in his mind that he wants to start up a new business for whatever reason? Why should we do that? Second, it is not fair for the competitors of that service.
March 26, 1993

Here is the instance I discovered about a year and a half or two years ago. I found evidence that Canada Post was sending letters to its customers, large mail users, saying roughly the following: "Fill up your postage machines now. In filling up your postage machines we will give you credit vouchers to be used for Priority Post courier". The courier service of course runs in competition with private enterprise and it is unregulated. By encouraging people to buy large amounts of postage stamps to load up their postage machines in their offices, some of the revenue of that was used to cross-subsidize the other. That cannot be right. There is no agency to review this.
Canada Post needs a form of CRTC of the post office. Maybe the member across does not think that is necessary. That agency exists in the United States. There is a watchdog to review its postal service.
With the present unpopularity of our Canadian postal system in Canada, if there were no other reason, that alone would be sufficient reason why we would want to avail ourselves of the kind of agency I am suggesting.
More than anything else, the Marchment committee report some years ago recommended the creation of such an agency. The Marchment committee report recommended in 1985 the creation of an agency like this.
In 1988, as I said, the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs announced that there would be a third party review of Canada Post Corporation's rates and services.
I brought to your attention that on June 27, 1988 the minister responsible at the time indicated that this was "an idea whose time has come". Finally, on August 15, 1988 the minister actually introduced the bill, a bill which is identical to the one I am proposing to the House today.
This has been an idea heavily promoted by the Conservative government with the support of all parties in this House. Yes, some of us said we wanted the bill that the government proposed to be a little stronger and so on in order to ensure that it had all the strength possible, but we were in favour of the idea.
What this House may not know is that the postal services review board, as proposed in this act, actually was constituted and its first chairman was Mr. Alan
Private Members' Business
Marchment. It was called the Postal Services Review Committee as an interim step until the act was passed. It even reported to a committee of this House.
I have in hand the February 6, 1990 report of Alan Marchment, chairman of the Postal Services Review Committee, to the House of Commons Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Government Operations. It is quite a lengthy report in which he recommended a number of improvements to Canada's postal service.
What did the government do? In the next budget after that report, it cancelled the Postal Services Review Committee. I have to ask the question, why? Could it be that the committee told the government what it did not want to hear? Could it be, I ask the parliamentary secretary who I see waving to me, that the government did not have the money to continue it? If it did not have the money, why did it create the thing to start with? It was in operation for only a year.
Postal users pay a lot of money for their postage stamps. Are they not entitled to have a say? Right now they do not have any.
Here is the recommendation of our committee in April 1990. The Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Government Operations Committee of the House of Commons in its report "Moving the Mail" said, and I quote here from our report: "The committee also believes that it is necessary to balance the interests of the regulator and the corporation by supporting both the review agency's need for information and the corporation's need for protection for commercially sensitive data. At the same time, we are of the view that as much information as possible about postal rates and services must remain in the public domain".
We even made recommendations about how much information Canada Post had to give to this committee. I continue: "The committee therefore recommends that anybody exercising review powers of Canada Post have legal authority to compel Canada Post to provide all information necessary for it to conduct an effective review in accordance with its mandate. Secondly, while ensuring that as much information as possible remain public, provision be made where necessary to allow the review agency to receive information from Canada Post in confidence".

March 26, 1993
Private Members' Business
This is a recommendation that received the unanimous approval of a committee of this House.
I say today to the government that it should speak in favour of the bill, provide its unanimous consent to allow the bill to go to a legislative committee for review and enactment as soon as possible.
I ask this of our colleagues across the way. They know it is the right thing to do. They know such a structure exists for other kinds of monopoly services in Canada. They know such a structure exists for postal services elsewhere in the world. They know the same bill and the same structure have even existed under the present government.
I ask them to do for once what Canadian consumers want, to stop this nonsense, stop their partisan way of looking at things, and think of the best interest of the Canadian consumer who is paying handsomely for postal services that are administered in an arbitrary and sometimes most unfair way.

Madam Speaker, I come to the debate today with some different feelings. I have as much concern for the post office service in Canada as the member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, but I also see the other side.
I came here today with strong feelings about the bill. Yet the member's argument has been quite persuasive for me in terms of the many viewpoints. The history of the situation intrigued me. At one time the government proposed a board, had a board and ended that board's life. In fact the party the member represents today at one time created the new independent post office structure on purpose so that it could compete in the communications area freely and without government intervention.
In spite of the argument of the hon. member for Glengarry- Prescott-Russell I propose that we do not support the bill today. Canada Post is one of the major players in the communications field. If we put on more regulations that increase costs and create obstruction we
will simply curtail its ability to function in the interests of the Canadian economy and Canadian businesses.
Most members will recall that in 1981 the previous government, with the agreement of all parties, converted the old money losing post office department into a Crown corporation. At the time the minister of the Crown of the day, the member for Papineau-Saint-Mi-chel, emphasized that the independence of the management of the new Canada Post would be one of the most important elements of making the new organization successful. As reported in the Debates for April 9, 1981, almost 12 years ago, he said at third reading of Bill C-42:
The Canadian public will be getting a better service and, above all, management will have a chance to give a full measure of their ability knowing that they are in full control of the situation and that they do not depend on decisions in other departments in order to provide an efficient management of the Canadian postal service.
It interests me that the hon. member speaking for his party today, or perhaps it is just for himself in Private Members' Hour, has taken a contrary stand to that of people in his own party 12 years ago as much as perhaps we have done in the time since the board has been in place.
The former minister also dealt directly with the question of setting regulated rates for postal services. He appeared to be quite satisfied, and apparently members on all sides of the House on that day were as well, that the arrangements in the legislation for establishing rates would allow for an adequate public input. The legislation which still exists to this day provides for a six-month notification of proposed changes. New rates are published in The Canada Gazette for everyone to see. Interested Canadians can forward their comments directly to the minister responsible for Canada Post. They take advantage of that right to a great extent. It may be because they are not effective in overturning the rates that they do not feel their requests are heard but I know they are. Certainly I see them coming through my office. Cabinet must still approve the rates. It is not totally done by the post office. There is an elected group of people who make decisions and exercise final control over postal rates.

The level of review of Canada Post rates at this time is already extensive. The hon. member now believes it is necessary to remove Canada Post's independence. He said in his opening statement that Canada Post was unregulated. He wants to impose more regulations. He wants to make it more difficult for Canada Post to function. In present circumstances his idea is not warranted.
The result of removing the management of the post office from interference by government has been to generate positive benefits for Canadians. We do not want to go back to the time when every postmaster was appointed on the recommendation of a member of Parliament. I understand there was one small community in the east coast represented by a Liberal cabinet minister of many years ago which had five postmasters for one town of 1,500 people. We do not want to see that kind of thing happen again.
Let me say a bit about the positive accomplishments of Canada Post. Hon. members are aware, because they will have been mailing many letters back to their ridings and perhaps across Canada, of the quick turnaround right now in Canada Post. We have had episodes since 1984 when I was first elected of it taking 10 days to get a letter to my riding in the centre of Ontario and 10 days to come back. It was a 20-day turnaround. Now the turnaround is so quick I almost wonder if the first letter ever went out. I will write it on a Monday, mail it to my riding and have an answer back in my office on the Hill before the end of the week. That is a very common occurrence.
Once in a while one or two letters take off or a bag of mail gets hooked up and those hit the headlines. The service from Canada Post for first-class mail has been very good in the last few years.
Postal rates have gone up, when measured in absolute terms by hours of work. The cost of a stamp compared to relative costs in other parts of the world is among the lowest in the industrialized world. This is a definite competitive advantage for Canadians.
On the labour front we have had many occurrences of difficult labour-management negotiations. Canada Post and major unions representing all the employees have signed settlements which will run for the next several years. We are into a period of calm and quiet where delivery can be the main objective of Canada Post.
Private Members' Business
Following several decades of losses in places where we had to pump in money to keep it going and where the general taxpayers as a whole covered for the users, Canada Post is now in a positive cash flow. Some of the money put in to cover deficits in the past is now returning to the Government of Canada. While doing this Canada Post has found new and innovative ways to expand service and make postal service available and affordable to more and more Canadians.
The hon. member might, through this legislation, take us back to the days when Canada Post was a department of government and introduce again the level of political interference which I spoke about a little earlier. The deliberate arm's length relationship with management as envisioned by the former minister might be destroyed if this legislation is brought in. A return to the old ways of doing things is simply another reversal of policy and an attempt to establish another level of costly bureaucracy.
I do not think the hon. member recognizes that competition in the marketplace has also been very influential in the progress Canada Post has achieved. I am told by constituents that because of electronic communication the post office is dead. Despite that, the amount of products delivered by the post office seems to increase yearly. Direct competition for parcel, courier, faxes and other products has forced the post office ahead. Technological electronics and the communication field have had a positive impact in motivating Canada Post to improve in all areas.
Canada Post competes and competition forces improvements. It has a stronger effect on its service than any board that would delay decisions and bring in committee style management could ever hope to introduce.
The member is proposing through this legislation to burden in this competitive field the business of Canada Post with the cost of a new regulatory regime. In trying to do this I am sure the committee would want to know the plans of Canada Post and in consultation with the board would expose the plans of Canada Post to its competitors. This would make it very difficult for Canada Post to respond rapidly to a changing market environment. The effect in Canada Post would be to eliminate it from competitive markets and increase the cost of postal service. The proposition is unfair and not in the best interest of Canadians.

March 26, 1993
Private Members' Business
Finally Canada Post has already seen the wisdom of consultation and has had a forum of postal services users express their concerns. The value to both the corporation and its customers is obvious.
The corporation decided to establish postal service customer councils. In preparing for this speech I learned about the councils today. I had not realized they were there. Perhaps that says they should be more prominent or more evident. I know through these councils, through approaches to members of Parliament which occur regularly, and through letters to the minister there is already an effective scrutiny of the tariffs charged by Canada Post. It also has a customer service initiative. Together with the 10 regional customer councils these are now a model for other Canadians companies.
Implementing the bill would be a step backward. The proposition of the Ottawa member would add a burden to the current postal services. It would not be in the interest of Canadians. Political interference, second guessing management, distorting competitive balances while adding unnecessary cost and bureaucracy are not conducive to a healthy and viable postal service for all Canadians. For these reasons I cannot support the proposed bill.

Madam Speaker, I rise to speak on the bill put forward by my colleague, the member for Glengarry-Prescott- Russell. I am the seconder of the bill.
Despite the comments of my worthy colleague from Perth-Wellington-Waterloo I am very much in support of the bill. I must say I have the greatest respect for that member. I listened very closely to his comments. I believe I detected in the thread of his presentation a certain willingness. If not to accept the major thrust of the bill, his preliminary comments indicated that he a certain sympathy. I do not know if these were exact words but certainly my impression from listening to him was that he understood where the member proposing the bill was coming from. He had certain affinities with the principle of the bill. Then he went on to say that because of government interference, political interference, and the possibility of regulatory agencies or review boards slowing down the service of Canada Post he could not support it.
I found that very difficult to understand. The organization is operating properly, professionally and with skill,
alacrity and efficiency. The member gave it good accolades. I agree we do have complaints from time to time with Canada Post, but by and large compared with the postal services of other countries and their per capita expenditure relative to ours we fare pretty well.
That is not the point today. I do not believe there is any system in the world that could not be improved on. I believe that Canada Post can be improved on. I am going to give the reasons for the main principles of why I believe in this and why I feel the way I do.
I have had occasion, as I am sure every single member of Parliament in this House has, to deal with Canada Post on several issues. The most frequent and recurring one is the corporate plan of Canada Post to shut down 5,221 post offices, not in urban Canada, but in rural Canada.
I understand this year it plans to close down over 250 post offices and the principle being used is when a natural opportunity occurs. This means when the postmaster or postmistress of a post office serving the smaller rural communities is about to retire, the Canada Post plan is to bring in a system that will change the post office. It will bring in either retail post offices or supermailboxes as they are called. I think it is a terrible misnomer. I do not think there is anything super about them at all.
It is a paradox when the hon. member who last spoke said he was not going to support my hon. colleague's bill because of the possibility and fear of political interference.
If there is any time for a review board to have some authority and watch what is called the efficiency of this organization, it is called into here and I will give the reason.
The member says he is afraid of political interference. Only three days ago I received a response from Canada Post, a three-page letter in turn, responding to a request that I had made regarding a rural post office in my riding. It was going to close because of a natural opportunity. The officials came down from Canada Post in January. It was right after Christmas. They listened to what everybody had to say, paid absolutely no attention and went back and said they were going to shut the post office down.

I wrote asking them to hang on. I was looking for fairness and balance. The thrust of my letter was that in the area of the Prime Minister's riding there were five rural post offices in which the natural opportunity had come up. One served a community of 121 people. It had to go out not once but twice and it is still looking for a postmaster or postmistress to operate that post office. The hon. member has the gall to say he does not want to support this bill because fear of political interference.
Everyone can draw their own conclusions from that. If that is the principle on why the hon. member is not supporting my hon. colleague's bill, then I think it is a pretty weak principle. I think he is dealing from a very, very distorted deck of cards and as a fiddler is playing very much out of tune.
I have citations here. My hon. colleague has given me tons of substantiations. I could stay here in the House as long as I would be permitted and give the testimony of those people. Who should know better than members in the House that there is a need and a necessity for such a board? I am going to quote one and I believe he is an authority.
On February 6, three years ago, Alan Marchment, the chairman of the then Postal Services Review Committee made a statement to the Standing Committee of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Government Operations of which my hon. colleague is a member. He said: "It is in the interest of the Canadian public to have a forum where rate and service charges must be reviewed publicly. As the relationship between Canada Post and the government becomes more arm's length, the need for a public return process increases". I understand Mr. Marchment is saying that if this kind of a review committee is implemented, the possibility of political interference will be reduced, not increased.
What is the purpose of the CRTC? I do not have its mandate here, but the purpose of the CRTC is to look at how radio and TV stations are licensed and to make sure the government cannot politically interfere. I am a great believer in democracy like all of us, but I have witnessed in the last four and half years the closure and time-allocated debates on important issues. We had one recently
Private Members' Business
on the unemployment insurance bill. When we get the situation in our country with a majority like the present government has, it can use its ramrod and jackboot measures as long as it wants. Our political system allows it. There are no checks and balances that would prevent it from happening.
This is the perfect example of a Crown corporation that has been the subject of considerable, and I would say sometimes acrimonious, discussion in this House, in correspondence, in town hall meetings and in political rallies. It is an excellent opportunity for the government to show faith and to say: "Okay, we have nothing to hide. We are quite prepared to allow a review committee to be established to look into the rate and service charges". It should do this in order to dispel any rumours that perhaps the postal rates are subsidizing an aspect of Canada Post that by government order should be precluded because it is in fact in competition with industry. God knows, industry needs every break it can get today.
I am not going to quote what they said, but in addition to that man who has credibility and recognition in the area on which he commented, there was the Nielsen task force, a considerable task force in 1985, the second year of the mandate of this government and consumer and corporate affairs in 1988. They also made recommendations.
How did the government respond to some pretty authoritative people and authorities in making proposals which essentially formed the core of my hon. colleague's bill? In 1990 the government did away with the postal service review board. To top it all off, the minister responsible for Canada Post said: "Oh, I favour this hands-off approach regarding the closing of rural post offices and mail delivery standards and the like".
However, I want to say that because there is no review board or other watch-dog I am going back to Canada Post and saying: "In your very learned three-page response to my question you did not address the question as to why in the Prime Minister's riding the principle of natural opportunity has not been applied in the same way as it is being applied in my area and in others".

March 26, 1993
Private Members' Business
I want to conclude by saying that everything my hon. colleague says about this bill I like, but the defence of not doing it I did not like. It did not make any sense. In fact the remarks of the hon. member from the other side convinced me even more that we should all support this outstanding and very timely bill.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council and Minister Responsible for Constitutional Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, thank you for giving me the opportunity to address you and the Canadian people this afternoon on this bill presented by my hon. colleague from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. I respect him a lot, although I cannot support such a motion for now.
I do not know what makes us politicians want to stick our noses into something that is going better all the time or going well, except to make political capital, even if it is only for as long as we speak in the House of Commons.
Canada Post had two important governmental decisions to make since it was created. When Andre Ouellet was the minister responsible for Canada Post, he made the first decision to privatize the postal system. It was a good decision.
Why did the government want to privatize the postal system then? It was to take from the House of Commons all sorts of decisions that were to be made about postal services and rates and other matters.
The other good decision about Canada Post was made after 1984-85, when the minister, Harvie Andre, told them: "Too bad, but starting now, you will have to cover your costs and come up with a corporate plan so that Canada Post will not depend on the government every year for the $200, $400 or $500 million you need to balance your budget".
One thing is clear, Madam Speaker. Why do we have postal services? To take a product and send it somewhere else at the lowest possible cost. Before, we would send the product somewhere else, but sometimes that was expensive and this was discussed in the House of Commons. Taxpayers watching us said there was no way they would pay 45 cents, so we told them we would charge 20 cents for sending the item and the government
would subsidize the remaining 25 cents. It still came out of the taxpayers pocket, but that didn't matter.
Basically providing postal services means taking a product and sending it somewhere else as quickly as possible and at the lowest possible cost. In 1985 the government told the Canada Post Corporation that the lowest possible cost of sending a product to Vancouver, for instance, was the real shipping cost. In other words, do not count on the government to subsidize potential deficits.
Of course there was a risk because Canada Post was practically in a monopoly position and people were afraid it would become a monopoly and would make decisions without regard for the interests of the general public. However that was not the case. It did not become a monopoly, on the contrary. Personally I think that soon we will have fewer and fewer post offices, unfortunately perhaps in terms of the federal presence. Why? Because it is not a monopoly. Look around Ottawa or Montreal or other major Canadian cities and see the services of priority post as well as those of other companies being used every day. I am thinking of Federal Express, Purolator and United Parcel Service, and they even have aeroplanes with their own logo to carry the mail. There is no longer a monopoly as there was before.
Second, we now have fax machines. Some post offices could close altogether and use fax machines to send the same letters, provided the addressee has a machine as well. We no longer have a government monopoly, but a Crown corporation competing with other companies with different prices and costs.
We are still sympathetic to consultation, but consultation is not necessarily what people will do because the decisions made concerning Canada Post always lead to emotional situations. Just look at what is happening right near Riviere-du-Loup, where the people are rising up against Canada Post because it wants to close the post office. Any platform is good. If there were an advisory board to review this decision, I am not sure the debate would be more elevated or more dignified because it would be in the House of Commons.
The place to do it is in the municipality concerned. That is an excellent forum for it. That is the only place for someone supposedly defending the rights of that community to seek a party's nomination and stand for election. Federal elections will be held very soon. All that is good for visibility.
March 26, 1993

Advisory boards lead to consultations, which often arouse appetites that cannot be satisfied. People do not want consultation but participation.
I must take my product and send it at the lowest possible cost in the least possible time. When Canada Post became a corporation and was told to cover its costs, it understood one thing. It realized that to cover its costs, it must provide better service. They now have a prestigious independent firm, Ernst and Young, that conducts surveys every two or three months, I believe, to find out how satisfied Canadians are with the postal service.
Madam Speaker, it is a good thing you are seated because what I am about to tell you could be quite staggering. This survey showed that 98 per cent of the mail is presently delivered on time. That is good. In fact, it is great. This means it takes two days within the same town, three between major cities of the same province and four to reach other centers across the country. That is excellent and cost is factored into it. There are people who complain about the cost of stamps these days. There are still people in this country who want to be able to mail a letter for five cents. That is just not possible any more.
If you examine the situation in industrialized countries that have faced up to their responsibilities regarding their postal systems, you realize that the price in Canada is among the lowest for a service which is fast in most cases. Granted, there will be problems and it is those we always hear about. Inevitably some time, some place a letter will get lost.
Last week I received at home a letter completely tom in two, probably by the machine. It happened to me once in the eight years I have lived at that address. It was an accident. I could have brought that letter to the House and said: "This is outrageous. Look at what happened to that letter". In a sense I was happy because it was the electrician's bill and the part that was tom was the one showing the amount payable. I called my electrical contractor, Paul Bouchard, and told him: "Mr. Bouchard, I received a nice apology from Canada Post but your bill has been tom to bits. You will have to send me a new one". I received the new bill as well.
Private Members' Business
I live in Beauhamois, a small town with a population of some 7,000. The letter carrier service was granted to Beauhamois at a time when the town was developing. It is simply marvellous to have someone bring your letters home five days a week. Beauhamois was promised a great development and its population grew to 10,000 before it fell back to 7,000. Saint-Timothee, a town located five or six miles from Beauhamois, experienced significant growth during the last five or six years. It is now bigger than Beauhamois and wants letter carrier service and cannot get it. My time is almost up? I could go on for at least two hours. They cannot get the service. Do you know why I have the privilege to have mail delivered at my doorstep five days a week, and the people in Saint-Timothee do not? It is often because of what is written in collective agreements. I would be happy to receive my mail only three or two times a week and share the service with other people. But that is not how it works.
Advisory committees or committees such as the one we will be creating to review services which are becoming more and more competitive and challenged could improve matters. Also, and I will conclude with this, when the project was developed, we had the money to pay for it. Nowadays we do not have that kind of money and we can only afford to increase the service. Quality is what we will be judged on and Canadians will support us on this.

Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to participate in this debate. I want to say I am certainly in support of this bill put forth by the member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell.
I have to take some issue with the member for Beauhamois-Salaberry who just spoke. I think that what he is saying clearly demonstrates his government's misguided view. Surely it is not going to be helpful to the people across this country, particularly in rural Canada. He talks about being from a small town of 7,000. In my riding I am talking about communities of 100, 200, 500, maybe 2,000. There was a time in this country when the post office was here to provide a service for Canadians.

March 26, 1993
Private Members' Business
That is no longer the case. It is here to make a profit. If the member thinks we should be having a-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That's not a bad idea.

He says it is not a bad but a good idea to run it at a profit. If we are going to have a progressive country that encourages competition and development there are some services that we need, certainly in places like Saskatchewan. Since this government has been involved with deregulation and transportation and with this attitude toward postal service, Saskatchewan has been suffering and businesses have been suffering in that province.
If we ran everything strictly on a profit basis there would not be anybody living in rural Saskatchewan because there would be nothing there to maintain them. It has been of economic benefit to this country to maintain a viable rural infrastructure in this country. One of the reasons this country has a problem now is because of the policies of his government that have caused much of the demise of rural Canada.
Just to make some comments. He says that it cannot afford the services. Canada Post is making a profit these days. Canada Post has come to communities in my riding and said it is going to give them better service. It is going to close their corporate post office and, although it says it will consult, they either get a retail postal outlet or green boxes.
Communities have told me that if Canada Post wanted to come into their communities and break even they would have been willing to work with it. Briercrest said it did not need service six days a week. It gets its post six days a week and would take it five days a week if it would then break even. The town of Simpson in my riding offered Canada Post a free building if it could keep its post office. Communities have offered the help of volunteers to assist the postmaster or postmistress. Canada Post has refused them all. That is because it is not interested in providing service for Canadians, but in selling Canada Post. That is what it is interested in doing.
If we are going to allow it to be taken over by a private corporation that is going to run it at a profit then it is not going to have post offices in many areas of rural Canada
pure and simple. That is because it is a business that is there to make a profit. I understand that is the hon. member's view. If that is his view, I submit if we are to have a healthy economy that is going to develop and allow businesses to establish and communities to maintain themselves and grow then we need some services. It should be the responsibility of this government to provide those services.
I want to speak more specifically to the bill itself. The idea of setting up a services review board was introduced by the then Minister for Consumer and Corporate Affairs, the government House leader, who said in a news release back in 1988: "Setting up a system that gives Canadians a voice in the planning of postal rates and services is an idea whose time has come. Now that Canada Post is breaking even and revenues are coming out of the pockets of postal users, customers have a right to a say in both national and local issues". I agree with that. That is a good approach. They should have a say in those issues.
The body was actually set up for a period of time under Alan Marchment, who actually made some reports. When these reports came out they were very critical of the government. Suddenly the whole atmosphere changed, the committee disappeared and was gone.
If we are going to maintain some service in this country we cannot simply allow a government to tell Canada Post that its bottom line is to get rid of as many rural post offices and urban post offices as it possibly can and to privatize as many post offices as it possibly can in order to sell the Canada Post business.
It may be okay for the city of Toronto, I do not know. It may be fine there because there will be a lot of competition. Purolator will go into Toronto. Purolator will work in the area of southern Ontario and certain areas in Quebec. I would like the hon. member to go up to northwestern Quebec, to Abitibi, Normetal, Dupuis and those places, and see what they would think about losing their post offices up there. Go into rural Saskatchewan, go into any part of rural Canada, go into rural Newfoundland. These are areas that need a service. As Canadians we should have a right to expect some basic services in this country. Certainly Canada Post is one of them.
March 26, 1993

If the attitude of this government had been adopted in the history of this country, certainly places like Saskatchewan would not have developed the way they have. It was because of a desire to provide transportation, for example, that the Saskatchewan transportation company was set up by an NDP government because Greyhound would not go to some small communities. Yet these small communities where there are businesses, and service stations needed that service.
I know as a lawyer working in small town Saskatchewan I certainly could not afford to run my practice having mail two days a week. It would not work.
I think the bill put forth by the member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell is the right approach. I think the position put forth by the government some four or five years ago is a good approach. Everything in this country simply cannot run on free enterprise and bottom line competition. That is not how this country was built. It was John A. Macdonald with the national policy. If John A. Macdonald had believed in free enterprise we would never have settled the west because that was a program to encourage development in certain regions of the country, namely western Canada.
To have that sort of attitude simply is not going to work, especially when we live in a country that is the second largest in the world geographically. Thirty-three per cent of Canadians, one in three Canadians, live in three cities: Montreal, Toronto, Vancouver. Forty-seven per cent live in nine cities.
Private Members' Business
If we are going to maintain some kind of infrastructure, we have to be committed to providing services to rural Canadians through transportation, postal service, health care delivery, education, and a whole host of issues. That has to be the commitment.
Yes, we have to cut down our deficit. Yes, our debt is too high. Absolutely. We can do that and still provide some of the services. Certainly Canada Post does not have to be privatized. It is making a profit. It is providing a service. However, it is now taking an attitude that is ripping the heart out of rural Canada.
I want to say in closing that I support this bill. I think it is the right approach to proceed with. I just regret that we are only going to have one hour of debate on this bill. It will die on the Order Paper. That is a tragedy. It certainly deserves far more debate and far more interest than that.
